往后许多年，也许几百年，我们士兵住过的那些村舍和谷仓，都会留着大战中英军驻扎的痕迹和记忆。后来开上战场、跨进鬼魂世界的男孩们，把自己的名字刻在木梁上，在刷白的墙上涂写宣言：列兵约翰·约翰逊是个混蛋；某营是一窝恶棍；德皇比尔将上绞架——还配上肖像和寓意画，画得潦草，却生动有力。

===Original===

The soldier in the house learned quite a lot of French, with which he made his needs understood by the elderly woman who cooked for his officers’ mess. He could say, with a fine fluency, “*Où est le* blooming *couteau*?” or “*Donnez-moi le* bally *fourchette, s’il vous plaît*, madame.” It was not beyond his vocabulary to explain that “*Les pommes de terre frites* are *absolument* all right if only madame will *tenir ses cheveux* on.” In the courtyards of ancient farmhouses, so old in their timbers and gables that the Scottish bodyguard of Louis XI may have passed them on their way to Paris, modern Scots with khaki-covered kilts pumped up the water from old wells, and whistled “I Know a Lassie” to the girl who brought the cattle home, and munched their evening rations while Sandy played a “wee bit” on the pipes to the peasant-folk who gathered at the gate. Such good relations existed between the cottagers and their temporary guests that one day, for instance, when a young friend of mine came back from a long spell in the trenches (his conversation was of dead men, flies, bombs, lice, and hell), the old lady who had given him her best bedroom at the beginning of the war flung her arms about him and greeted him like a long-lost son. To a young Guardsman, with his undeveloped mustache on his upper lip, her demonstrations were embarrassing.

It was one of the paradoxes of the war that beauty lived but a mile or two away from hideous squalor. While men in the lines lived in dugouts and marched down communicating trenches thigh-high, after rainy weather, in mud and water, and suffered the beastliness of the primitive earthmen, those who were out of the trenches, turn and turn about, came back to leafy villages and drilled in fields all golden with buttercups, and were not too uncomfortable in spite of overcrowding in dirty barns.

---

===Chinese===

住在人家屋里的士兵学了不少法语，用它让给军官食堂做饭的老太太明白自己的需要。他能流利地说：「Où est le 该死的 couteau（刀在哪儿）？」或「Donnez-moi le 他妈的 fourchette, s'il vous plaît, madame（劳驾太太，给我叉子）」。让他解释「Les pommes de terre frites（炸薯条）absolument（绝对）没得挑，只要太太把 cheveux（头发）束紧些」，也不超出他的词量。在古老农庄的院里——梁木和山墙老得说不定路易十一的苏格兰卫队进军巴黎时曾从旁经过——现代的苏格兰人，卡其布罩着格子裙，从老井里压水，朝赶牛回家的姑娘吹《我认识一个姑娘》，嚼着晚饭的口粮，桑迪在门口聚拢的庄稼人面前，用风笛吹上一小段。村舍人家同这些临时房客之间交情好到这样：比如有一天，我的一个年轻朋友从长驻的战壕回来（他张口就是死人、苍蝇、炸弹、虱子和地狱），战争开始时把自己最好的卧室让给他的老太太张开双臂搂住他，像迎一个失散多年的儿子。对一个上唇还没蓄出小胡子的年轻近卫兵，这一番亲热叫他受窘。

这场战争的悖论之一是：美，离可怕的狼藉只有一两英里。线上的人住地洞、蹚交通壕——雨后泥水齐大腿——受着原始穴居人的兽境；轮下来的人则回到绿荫的村庄，在满地毛茛金黄的田野里操练，虽然挤在肮脏谷仓里，倒也不算太难受。

---

===Original===

There was more than comfort in some of the headquarters where our officers were billeted in French châteaux. There was a splendor of surroundings which gave a graciousness and elegance to the daily life of that extraordinary war in which men fought as brutally as in prehistoric times. I knew scores of such places, and went through gilded gates emblazoned with noble coats of arms belonging to the days of the Sun King, or farther back to the Valois, and on my visits to generals and their staffs stood on long flights of steps which led up to old mansions, with many towers and turrets, surrounded by noble parks and ornamental waters and deep barns in which five centuries of harvests had been stored. From one of the archways here one might see in the mind’s eye Mme. de Pompadour come out with a hawk on her wrist, or even Henri de Navarre with his gentlemen-at-arms, all their plumes alight in the sun as they mounted their horses for a morning’s boar-hunt.

It was surprising at first when a young British officer came out and said, “Toppin’ morning,” or, “Any news from the Dardanelles?” There was something incongruous about this habitation of French châteaux by British officers with their war-kit. The strangeness of it made me laugh in early days of first impressions, when I went through the rooms of one of those old historic houses, well within range of the German guns with a brigade major. It was the Château de Henencourt, near Albert.

“This is the general’s bedroom,” said the brigade major, opening a door which led off a gallery, in which many beautiful women of France and many great nobles of the old regime looked down from their gilt frames.

===Chinese===

我们军官驻扎的那些法式城堡，有些不止是舒适。环境的排场给那场非同寻常的战争的日常生活添了优雅——那战争里人们打得同史前一样野蛮。这样的地方我认得几十处：穿过镌着太阳王时代、或更早的瓦卢瓦时代贵族纹章的镀金大门，去拜访将军和他们的参谋时，踏上通向古老府邸的长长的台阶——塔楼角楼成群，围着一派气派的园林、水景，和深深的谷仓——里面存过五个世纪的收成。在这些拱门下，你尽可以想象德·蓬巴杜夫人托着鹰走出来，甚至纳瓦拉的亨利带着他的武士，翎羽在太阳里发亮，上马去晨猎野猪。

一个年轻的英国军官走出来，说一句「顶好的早晨」，或者「达达尼尔有消息么？」起初总叫人一愣。英国军官带着行头住进法兰西城堡，透着一种不般配。早年的第一印象里，这种怪曾叫我发笑——那时我同一位旅参谋长穿过一座老宅的房间，它完全在德军炮火射程之内。那是阿尔贝附近的埃纳古尔城堡。

「这是将军的卧室，」旅参谋长说，推开一扇门，门开在一道长廊上，长廊里，法兰西的许多美丽女人、旧制度的许多大贵族，从镀金的画框里俯视下来。

===Original===

The general had a nice bed to sleep in. In such a bed Mme. du Barry might have stretched her arms and yawned, or the beautiful Duchesse de Mazarin might have held her morning levee. A British general, with his bronzed face and bristly mustache, would look a little strange under that blue-silk canopy, with rosy cherubs dancing overhead on the flowered ceiling. His top-boots and spurs stood next to a Louis Quinze toilet-table. His leather belts and field-glasses lay on the polished boards beneath the tapestry on which Venus wooed Adonis and Diana went a-hunting. In other rooms no less elegantly rose-tinted or darkly paneled other officers had made a litter of their bags, haversacks, rubber baths, trench-boots, and puttees. At night the staff sat down to dinner in a salon where the portraits of a great family of France, in silks and satins and Pompadour wigs, looked down upon their khaki. The owner of the château, in whose veins flowed the blood of those old aristocrats, was away with his regiment, in which he held the rank of corporal. His wife, the Comtesse de Henencourt, managed the estate, from which all the menservants except the veterans had been mobilized. In her own château she kept one room for herself, and every morning came in from the dairies, where she had been working with her maids, to say, with her very gracious smile, to the invaders of her house: “*Bon jour, messieurs! Ça va bien?*”

She hid any fear she had under the courage of her smile. Poor châteaux of France! German shells came to knock down their painted turrets, to smash through the ceilings where the rosy Cupids played, and in one hour or two to ruin the beauty that had lived through centuries of pride.

Scores of them along the line of battle were but heaps of brick-dust and twisted iron.

I saw the ruins of the Château de Henencourt two years after my first visit there. The enemy’s line had come closer to it and it was a target for their guns. Our guns﻿—heavy and light﻿—were firing from the back yard and neighboring fields, with deafening tumult. Shells had already broken the roofs and turrets of the château and torn away great chunks of wall. A colonel of artillery had his headquarters in the petit salon. His hand trembled as he greeted me.

“I’m not fond of this place,” he said. “The whole damn thing will come down on my head at any time. I think I shall take to the cellars.”

===Chinese===

将军有一张好床睡。在这样的床上，杜巴里夫人或许伸过懒腰打过哈欠，美丽的马扎兰公爵夫人或许临过她的晨觐。一位英国将军，古铜的脸，扎人的胡子，躺在那顶蓝绸华盖下、头顶天花板上玫瑰色小天使跳舞的花板下，看着有点怪。他的长筒靴和马刺立在一张路易十五的梳妆台旁。他的皮带和望远镜丢在磨亮的地板上，头顶的挂毯上维纳斯在挑逗阿多尼斯、狄安娜在行猎。别的房间里——一样雅致，或淡红、或深色板壁——别的军官把自己的背囊、干粮袋、橡胶浴盆、战壕靴和绑腿摊了一地。夜里，参谋们在客厅坐下吃饭，厅里挂着一个法兰西望族的画像，绫罗绸缎、蓬巴杜假发，俯视着他们的卡其布。城堡的主人——血管里流着那些老贵族的血——随他的团走了，军衔是下士。他的妻子埃纳古尔伯爵夫人打理着田庄，男仆除老弱外都征走了。她自家城堡里只留一间屋，每天早晨从牛棚里进来——她同女仆们一起干活——对占据她家的人们绽开极优雅的微笑：「日安，先生们！都好么？」

她把恐惧全藏进微笑的勇气底下。可怜的法兰西城堡啊！德国炮弹来撞倒它们彩绘的塔楼，砸穿玫瑰色丘比特嬉戏的天花板，一两个钟头里毁掉历经几个世纪骄傲的美。

战线沿路几十座城堡只剩砖粉和拧铁的堆。

头一次来访两年之后，我又见了埃纳古尔城堡的废墟。敌人的防线离它近了，它成了他们火炮的靶子。我们的炮——重炮轻炮——正从后院和邻近的田野里发射，震耳欲聋。炮弹已经砸破了城堡的屋顶和塔楼，撕走了大块墙体。一位炮兵上校把指挥部设在小客厅里。他迎我时手在抖。

「我不喜欢这地方，」他说。「这整座鬼东西随时会砸我头上。我想我得搬进地窖去。」

===Original===

We walked out to the courtyard and he showed me the way down to the vault. A shell came over the château and burst in the outhouses.

“They knocked out a 9.2 a little while ago,” said the colonel. “Made a mess of some heavy gunners.”

There was a sense of imminent death about us, but it was not so sinister a place as farther on, where a brother of mine sat in a hole directing his battery﻿ ﻿… The Countess of Henencourt had gone. She went away with her dairymaids, driving her cattle down the roads.

===Chinese===

我们走出去到院子里，他指给我下地窖的路。一发炮弹越过城堡，在附属建筑里炸开。

「不久前他们敲掉了一门九点二，」上校说。「把一队重炮兵弄得很惨。」

我们四周弥漫着死亡迫近的感觉，可它还不如更前面那地方阴森——我的一个兄弟就坐在那里的一个洞里指挥他的炮兵连……埃纳古尔伯爵夫人已经走了。她带着她的挤奶女工赶着牛沿大路去了。

### XII / 十二

### XII / 
===Original===

One of the most curious little schools of courage inhabited by British soldiers in early days was the village of Vaux-sur-Somme, which we took over from the French, who were our next-door neighbors at the village of Frise in the summer of ’15. After the foul conditions of the salient it seemed unreal and fantastic, with a touch of romance not found in other places. Strange as it seemed, the village garrisoned by our men was in advance of our trench lines, with nothing dividing them from the enemy but a little undergrowth﻿—and the queerest part of it all was the sense of safety, the ridiculously false security with which one could wander about the village and up the footpath beyond, with the knowledge that one’s movements were being watched by German eyes and that the whole place could be blown off the face of the earth﻿ ﻿… but for the convenient fact that the Germans, who were living in the village of Curlu, beyond the footpath, were under our own observation and at the mercy of our own guns.

That sounded like a fairytale to men who, in other places, could not go over the parapet of the first-line trenches, or even put their heads up for a single second, without risking instant death.

I stood on a hill here, with a French interpreter and one of his men. A battalion of loyal North Lancashires was some distance away, but after an exchange of compliments in an idyllic glade, where a party of French soldiers lived in the friendliest juxtaposition with the British infantry surrounding them﻿—it was a cheery bivouac among the trees, with the fragrance of a stew-pot mingling with the odor of burning wood﻿—the lieutenant insisted upon leading the way to the top of the hill.

He made a slight detour to point out a German shell which had fallen there without exploding, and made laughing comments upon the harmless, futile character of those poor Germans in front of us. They did their best to kill us, but oh, so feebly!

Yet when I took a pace toward the shell he called out, sharply, “*Ne touchez pas!*” I would rather have touched a sleeping tiger than that conical piece of metal with its unexploded possibilities, but bent low to see the inscriptions on it, scratched by French gunners with more recklessness of death. *Mort aux Boches* was scrawled upon it between the men’s initials.

===Chinese===

英军早期住过的最古怪的小小勇气学校之一，是索姆河畔沃村，一九一五年夏天我们从法国人手里接过来，他们是弗里兹村的紧邻。从突出部的污浊条件里过来，这里显得不真实、离奇，带着别处没有的一点浪漫。说来奇怪，我们士兵驻守的村子竟在我们的堑壕线之外，同敌人之间只隔一丛灌木——而整件事最古怪的是那种安全感，那种可笑的虚假太平：你可以在村里随便走，走上村外的小径，明知自己的一举一动都有德国眼睛看着，整个地方随时可以从地面上轰掉……只因有一个便利的事实：住在小径那头克尔吕村的德国人，处在我们自己的观察之下，任凭我们自己的炮摆布。

在别的地方，翻出一线战壕的胸墙、哪怕探头一秒钟都冒立毙之险的人们听来，这像童话。

我同一个法国译兵和他的一个兵站在山上。忠勇北兰开夏的一个营在一段距离外，但在林间一块田园诗的小空地上寒暄过之后——一小队法国士兵同围着他们的英国步兵毗邻而居，处得最友好——那是个林间的快活营地，炖锅的香味混着柴烟——中尉坚持领路上山顶。

他略绕了点路，指给我看一发落在那里没炸的德国炮弹，笑着评论我们面前那些可怜德国人的无害与无用。他们尽力想杀我们，可是啊，那么软！

可等我朝炮弹迈一步，他尖声喊：「别碰！」我宁可去摸一只睡虎，也不想碰那颗锥形金属和它未炸开的可能，但弯下腰细看上面的刻字——法国炮手刻的，比死亡还随便。Mort aux Boches（波希人该死）涂在姓名缩写中间。

===Original===

Then we came to the hill-crest and to the last of our trenches, and, standing there, looked down upon the villages of Vaux and Curlu, separated by a piece of marshy water. In the farthest village were the Germans, and in the nearest, just below us down the steep cliff, our own men. Between the two there was a narrow causeway across the marsh and a strip of woods half a rifle-shot in length.

Behind, in a sweeping semicircle round their village and ours, were the German trenches and the German guns. I looked into the streets of both villages as clearly as one may see into Clovelly village from the crest of the hill. In Vaux-sur-Somme a few British soldiers were strolling about. One was sitting on the windowsill of a cottage, kicking up his heels.

In the German village of Curlu the roadways were concealed by the perspective of the houses, with their gables and chimney-stacks, so that I could not see any passersby. But at the top of the road, going out of the village and standing outside the last house on the road, was a solitary figure﻿—a German sentry.

The French lieutenant pointed to a thin mast away from the village on the hillside.

“Do you see that? That is their flagstaff. They hoist their flag for victories. It wagged a good deal during the recent Russian fighting. But lately they have not had the cheek to put it up.”

This interpreter﻿—the Baron de Rosen﻿—laughed very heartily at that naked pole on the hill.

Then I left him and joined our own men, and went down a steep hill into Vaux, well outside our line of trenches, and thrust forward as an outpost in the marsh. German eyes could see me as I walked. At any moment those little houses about me might have been smashed into rubbish heaps. But no shells came to disturb the waterfowl among the reeds around.

And so it was that the life in this place was utterly abnormal, and while the guns were silent except for long-range fire, an old-fashioned mode of war﻿—what the adjutant of this little outpost called a “gentlemanly warfare,” prevailed. Officers and men slept within a few hundred yards of the enemy, and the officers wore their pajamas at night. When a fight took place it was a chivalrous excursion, such as Sir Walter Manny would have liked, between thirty or forty men on one side against somewhat the same number on the other.

===Chinese===

然后我们到了山顶，到了我们最后一条战壕，站在那里俯瞰沃村和克尔吕村，中间隔着一小片沼水。最远的村里是德国人，最近的村里，就在我们脚下的陡崖下，是我们自己的人。两村之间，是一道横过沼泽的窄堤和半枪长的一条树林。

后面，绕着他们的村子和我们的村子兜开一道半圆的，是德国人的战壕和德国人的炮。两村的街道我看得清清楚楚，像从山脊上看克利夫利村那么清楚。索姆河畔沃村里，几个英国兵在闲逛。一个坐在村舍的窗台上踢着脚跟。

德国人的克尔吕村里，路面被山墙和烟囱的透视挡住，我看不见行人。但在出村大路的顶头，站在路边最后一座房子外面，有孤零零一个人影——德国哨兵。

法国中尉指向山坡上离村的一根细杆。

「看见了么？那是他们的旗杆。打了胜仗就升旗。前一阵俄国战事里它晃得可欢。可近来他们没脸皮升了。」

这位译兵——德罗森男爵——对着山上那根光杆大笑。

随后我离开他，去找我们自己的人，顺着陡坡下到沃村——完全在我们战壕线外，作为沼泽里的前哨伸出去。我走动时德国眼睛看得见。随时，我四周那些小屋都可能被砸成瓦砾堆。可没有炮弹来搅扰苇丛里的水鸟。

于是这地方的生活彻底反常，炮声除远程火力外静默的时候，一种老式的战争方式——这个小前哨的副官称之为「君子之战」——风行着。官兵睡在离敌人几百码的地方，军官夜里穿睡衣。打起来的时候，那是一场骑士式的出游，沃尔特·曼尼爵士会喜欢的那种，三四十人对差不多同样数目的另一边。

===Original===

Our men used to steal out along the causeway which crossed the marsh﻿—a pathway about four feet wide, broadening out in the middle, so that a little redoubt or blockhouse was established there, then across a narrow drawbridge, then along the path again until they came to the thicket which screened the German village of Curlu.

It sometimes happened that a party of Germans were creeping forward from the other direction, in just the same way, disguised in parti-colored clothes splashed with greens and reds and browns to make them invisible between the trees, with brown masks over their faces. Then suddenly contact was made.

Into the silence of the wood came the sharp crack of rifles, the zip-zip of bullets, the shouts of men who had given up the game of invisibility. It was a sharp encounter one night when the Loyal North Lancashires held the village of Vaux, and our men brought back many German helmets and other trophies as proofs of victory. Then to bed in the village, and a good night’s rest, as when English knights fought the French, not far from these fields, as chronicled in the pages of that early war correspondent, Sir John Froissart.

All was quiet when I went along the causeway and out into the wood, where the outposts stood listening for any crack of a twig which might betray a German footstep. I was startled when I came suddenly upon two men, almost invisible, against the tree-trunks. There they stood, motionless, with their rifles ready, peering through the brushwood. If I had followed the path on which they stood for just a little way I should have walked into the German village. But, on the other hand, I should not have walked back again.﻿ ﻿…

When I left the village, and climbed up the hill to our own trenches again, I laughed aloud at the fantastic visit to that grim little outpost in the marsh. If all the war had been like this it would have been more endurable for men who had no need to hide in holes in the earth, nor crouch for three months below ground, until an hour or two of massacre below a storm of high explosives. In the village on the marsh men fought at least against other men, and not against invisible powers which belched forth death.

===Chinese===

我们的人常沿横过沼泽的堤道溜出去——那条道约四英尺宽，中间放宽，那里设了一个小堡垒或碉堡，再过一道窄吊桥，再沿小道走，直到遮住克尔吕村的那片树丛。

有时恰好一伙德国人从另一头同样地摸过来，穿洒了绿红棕各色的迷彩衣，好隐进树间，脸上蒙着棕色面罩。于是接触突然发生。

树林的寂静里响起步枪的脆响、子弹的嗖嗖、放弃了隐身游戏的人们的呐喊。忠勇北兰开夏驻沃村的某夜就有这样一场短兵相接，我们的人带回许多德国钢盔和别的战利品作胜利的凭证。然后回村里睡觉，睡一夜好觉，像当年英国骑士同法国人打仗那样——离这些田野不远，那位早期的随军记者让·傅华萨爵士的书页里记着这一切。

我沿堤道走进树丛时一切安静，前哨站在那里，听任何可能出卖德国脚步的枯枝声。我突然撞见两个人，几乎看不见，贴着树干。他们站在那里，一动不动，端着枪，透过灌木窥望。我要是顺着他们站的这条小道再走一小段，就走进德国村了。不过反过来，我也就走不回来了。……

离开村子、爬上山回到我们自己的战壕时，我为这场沼泽里森严小哨的奇幻之游放声笑了。倘若整个战争都这样，对于那些不必钻地洞、不必一连三个月蜷在地下等着高爆弹风暴里一两小时屠杀的人来说，倒好熬些。沼泽村子里的人至少是同人对阵，而不是同喷吐死亡的看不见的力量。

===Original===

It was part of the French system of “keeping quiet” until the turn of big offensives; a good system, to my mind, if not carried too far. At Frise, next door to Vaux, in a loop of the Somme, it was carried a little too far, with relaxed vigilance.

It was a joke of our soldiers to crawl on and through the reeds and enter the French line and exchange souvenirs with the sentries.

“Souvenir!” said one of them one day. “Bullet﻿—you know﻿—*cartouche*. Comprenny?”

A French poilu of Territorials, who had been dozing, sat up with a grin and said, “*Mais oui, mon vieux*,” and felt in his pouch for a cartridge, and then in his pockets, and then in the magazine of the rifle between his knees.

“*Fini!*” he said. “*Tout fini, mon p’tit camarade.*”

The Germans one day made a pounce on Frise, that little village in the loop of the Somme, and “pinched” every man of the French garrison. There was the devil to pay, and I heard it being played to the tune of the French *soixante-quinzes*, slashing over the trees.

Vaux and Curlu went the way of all French villages in the zone of war, when the battles of the Somme began, and were blown off the map.

===Chinese===

这是法国人那套「保持安静」直到大攻势轮次的体系的一部分；好体系，在我看来，只要别做过头。在沃村隔壁、索姆河河湾里的弗里兹，它就做得过了头，松了警惕。

我们的士兵爱开的一个玩笑，就是爬进钻过苇丛，进法国人的防线，同哨兵换纪念品。

「Souvenir（纪念品）！」一天其中一个说。「子弹——懂么——cartouche。明白？」

一个本土师的法国大兵本来在打盹，咧嘴坐起来说：「Mais oui, mon vieux（对呀，老伙计），」往弹药袋里摸子弹，又摸口袋，又摸膝盖中间那杆枪的弹仓。

「Fini（完了）！」他说。「Tout fini, mon p'tit camarade（全完了，小同志）。」

德国人有一天突袭了弗里兹，索姆河湾里那座小村，把法国守军「一锅端」了。这下炸了锅，我听见法国七五炮抡着树梢奏响了它的调子。

索姆河各战役打响之后，沃村和克尔吕村走了战区一切法国村子的老路，从地图上被轰掉了。

### XIII / 十三

### XIII / 
===Original===

At a place called the Pont de Nieppe, beyond Armentières﻿—a most “unhealthy” place in later years of war﻿—a bathing establishment was organized by officers who were as proud of their work as though they had brought a piece of paradise to Flanders. To be fair to them, they had done that. To any interested visitor, understanding the nobility of their work, they exhibited a curious relic. It was the Holy Shirt of Nieppe, which should be treasured as a memorial in our War Museum﻿—an object-lesson of what the great war meant to clean-living men. It was not a saint’s shirt, but had been worn by a British officer in the trenches, and was like tens of thousands of other shirts worn by our officers and men in the first winters of the war, neither better nor worse, but a fair average specimen. It had been framed in a glass case, and revealed, on its linen, the corpses of thousands of lice. That vermin swarmed upon the bodies of all our boys who went into the trenches and tortured them. After three days they were lousy from head to foot. After three weeks they were walking menageries. To English boys from clean homes, to young officers who had been brought up in the religion of the morning tub, this was one of the worst horrors of war. They were disgusted with themselves. Their own bodies were revolting to them. Scores of times I have seen battalions of men just out of battle stripping themselves and hunting in their shirts for the foul beast. They had a technical name for this hunter’s job. They called it “chatting.” They desired a bath as the hart panteth for the water-brooks, and baths were but a mirage of the brain to men in Flanders fields and beyond the Somme, until here and there, as at Nieppe, officers with human sympathy organized a system by which battalions of men could wash their bodies.

===Chinese===

在阿尔芒蒂耶尔那边一个叫尼普桥的地方——战争后期最「不卫生」的地方之一——军官们办起了一处浴场，为他们的工作骄傲，仿佛给佛兰德斯带来了一块天堂。平心而论，他们确实做到了。对懂得这工作之高贵的来访客人，他们展示一件古怪的遗物：尼普圣衣。它该当珍藏在我们的战争博物馆里——一件实物教具，让人看看大战对爱洁净的人意味着什么。它不是圣徒的衬衣，而是一位英国军官在战壕里穿过的，同战争头几个冬天我们官兵穿的成千上万件衬衣一样，不好也不坏，一个像样的平均样品。它装进了玻璃框，亚麻布上现出数千只虱子的尸首。那种害虫爬满我们所有进战壕的孩子的身体，折磨他们。三天之后，他们从头到脚生了虱。三星期之后，他们成了走路的兽群。对来自清洁家庭的英国男孩，对从小信奉晨浴之教的年轻军官，这是战争最坏的恐怖之一。他们厌恶自己。自己的身体让他们作呕。几十次，我看见刚出战的营的士兵脱光了在衬衣里搜捕那脏东西。这猎活他们有个行话的名字，叫「聊天」。他们渴望洗澡，像鹿渴慕溪水，而在佛兰德斯的田野、在索姆河外，澡对士兵只是脑中的幻影，直到这里那里，像尼普这里，有人情味的军官们组织起一套让成营的人能洗上身体的制度。

===Original===

The place in Nieppe had been a jute-factory, and there were big tubs in the sheds, and nearby was the water of the Lys. Boilers were set going to heat the water. A battalion’s shirts were put into an oven and the lice were baked and killed. It was a splendid thing to see scores of boys wallowing in those big tubs, six in a tub, with a bit of soap for each. They gave little grunts and shouts of joyous satisfaction. The cleansing water, the liquid heat, made their flesh tingle with exquisite delight, sensuous and spiritual. They were like children. They splashed one another, with gurgles of laughter. They put their heads under water and came up puffing and blowing like grampuses. Something broke in one’s heart to see them, those splendid boys whose bodies might soon be torn to tatters by chunks of steel. One of them remembered a bit of Latin he had sung at Stonyhurst: “*Asperges me, Domine, hyssopo, et mundabor; lavabis me, et super nivem dealbabor.*” (“Thou shalt sprinkle me with hyssop, O Lord, and I shall be cleansed; thou shalt wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow.”)

On the other side of the lines the Germans were suffering in the same way, lousy also, and they, too, were organizing bathhouses. After their first retreat I saw a queer name on a wooden shed: *Entlausunganstalt*. I puzzled over it a moment, and then understood. It was a new word created out of the dirt of modern war﻿—“Delousing station.”

===Chinese===

尼普这地方原是黄麻厂，棚子里有大木盆，近旁是利斯河的水。锅炉烧起来热水。全营的衬衣送进烤炉，虱子被烤死。看几十个男孩泡进那些大盆，一盆六个，一人一块肥皂，是件大快事。他们发出小小的哼声和快活的叫喊。洗净的水、温热的流，让他们皮肉酥酥地快活，肉体的也是灵魂的。他们像孩子。他们互相泼水，笑出咯咯声。他们把头闷进水里，钻出来呼哧呼哧像小海豚。看他们让人心里有什么东西断裂——这些出色的男孩，身体不久就可能被钢块撕成碎条。其中一个记起他在斯托尼赫斯特唱过的一句拉丁文：「Asperges me, Domine, hyssopo, et mundabor; lavabis me, et super nivem dealbabor.」（主啊，求你用牛膝草洁净我，我就干净；求你洗涤我，我就比雪更白。）

防线那一边，德国人受着同样的罪，同样生虱，他们也在办澡堂。他们第一次撤退后，我在一间木棚上见到一个怪词：Entlausunganstalt。我琢磨了一会儿，随即懂了。那是现代战争的污秽造出的一个新词——「灭虱站」。

### XIV / 十四

### XIV / 
===Original===

It was harvest-time in the summer of ’15, and Death was not the only reaper who went about the fields, although he was busy and did not rest even when the sun had flamed down below the belt of trees on the far ridge, and left the world in darkness.

On a night in August two of us stood in a cornfield, silent, under the great dome, staring up at the startling splendor of it. The red ball just showed above the far line of single trees which were black as charcoal on the edge of a long, straight road two miles away, and from its furnace there were flung a million feathers of flame against the silk-blue canopy of the evening sky. The burning colors died out in a few minutes, and the fields darkened, and all the corn-shocks paled until they became quite white, like rows of tents, under the harvest moon. Another night had come in this year of war.

Up Ypres way the guns were busy, and at regular intervals the earth trembled, and the air vibrated with dull, thunderous shocks.

“The moon’s face looks full of irony tonight,” said the man by my side. “It seems to say, ‘What fools those creatures are down there, spoiling their harvest-time with such a mess of blood!’ ”

The stars were very bright in some of those Flemish nights. I saw the Milky Way clearly tracked across the dark desert. The Pleiades and Orion’s belt were like diamonds on black velvet. But among all these worlds of light other stars, unknown to astronomers, appeared and disappeared. On the road back from a French town one night I looked Arras way, and saw what seemed a bursting planet. It fell with a scatter of burning pieces. Then suddenly the thick cloth of the night was rent with stabs of light, as though flashing swords were hacking it, and a moment later a finger of white fire was traced along the black edge of the far-off woods, so that the whole sky was brightened for a moment and then was blotted out by a deeper darkness﻿ ﻿… Arras was being shelled again, as I saw it many times in those long years of war.

===Chinese===

一九一五年夏天是收获的季节，在田野里走动的收割者不止死神一个，虽然他忙，太阳落到远山树带下面、把世界留给黑暗之后他也不歇。

八月的一个夜晚，我们两个人站在一块麦田里，沉默，在伟大的穹顶下，仰望它惊人的壮丽。红色的球刚刚冒出远处那排独树的线——它们黑得像炭，立在两英里外一条笔直长路的边上——从它的炉膛里，上百万根火焰的羽毛甩上傍晚丝绸蓝的穹幕。灼热的颜色几分钟内熄灭，田野暗下来，一垛垛麦捆褪成全白，像一排排帐篷，在收获的月亮底下。战争的这一年，又一夜来了。

伊普尔那边炮正忙，大地有规律地颤，空气随一阵阵沉闷的雷响震动。

「今晚月亮的脸充满讥诮，」我身边的人说。「它像在说：『底下的那些蠢货，拿这么一团血污糟蹋自己的收获季！』」

那些佛兰德斯夜晚，星星非常亮。我看见银河清晰地划过黑暗的荒漠。昴星团和猎户的腰带像黑天鹅绒上的钻石。可是在这些光的世界中间，另一些天文学家不识的星出现又消失。一天夜里从一座法国城回来的路上，我朝阿拉斯方向望，看见一颗像是崩裂的行星。它带着一蓬燃烧的碎片坠落。随即，夜之厚布忽然被光的戳刺撕开，仿佛闪烁的剑在砍它，片刻后，一根白火的指头描过远处树林的黑边，整个天空亮了一瞬，随即被更深的黑暗抹掉……阿拉斯又在挨炮了，漫长的战争年月里我见过它许多次。

===Original===

The darkness of all the towns in the war zone was rather horrible. Their strange, intense quietude, when the guns were not at work, made them dead, as the very spirit of a town dies on the edge of war. One night, as on many others, I walked through one of them with a friend. Every house was shuttered, and hardly a gleam came through any crack. No footstep, save our own, told of life. The darkness was almost palpable. It seemed to press against one’s eyeballs like a velvet mask. My nerves were so on edge with a sense of the uncanny silence and invisibility that I started violently at the sound of a quiet voice speaking three inches from my ear.

“*Halte! Qui va là?*”

It was a French sentry, who stood with his back to the wall of a house in such a gulf of blackness that not even his bayonet was revealed by a glint.

Another day of war came. The old beauty of the world was there, close to the lines of the bronzed cornfields splashed with the scarlet of poppies, and the pale yellow of the newly cut sheaves, stretching away and away, without the break of a hedge, to the last slopes which met the sky.

---

I stood in some of those harvest-fields, staring across to a slope of rising ground where there was no ripening wheat, and where the grass itself came to a sudden halt, as though afraid of something. I knew the reason of this, and of the long white lines of earth thrown up for miles each way. Those were the parapets of German trenches, and in the ditches below them were earthmen, armed with deadly weapons, staring out across the beauty of France and wondering, perhaps, why they should be there to mar it, and watching me, a little black dot in their range of vision, with an idle thought as to whether it were worth their while to let a bullet loose and end my walk. They could have done so easily, but did not bother. No shot or shell came to break through the hum of bees or to crash through the sigh of the wind, which was bending all the ears of corn to listen to the murmurous insect-life in these fields of France.

Close to me was a group of peasants﻿—a study for a painter like Millet. One of them shouted out to me, “*Voilà les Boches!*” waving his arm to left and right, and then shaking a clenched fist at them.

===Chinese===

战区里所有城镇的黑暗相当可怕。它们古怪而紧张的宁静——炮不干活的时候——使它们死了，像一座城的灵魂死在战争边缘上。一夜，同许多夜一样，我同朋友步行穿过其中一座。家家户户上了门板，缝里几乎不漏一线光。没有脚步声，除了我们自己的，说明生命。黑暗几乎摸得着。它像一副天鹅绒面具压上人的眼球。诡异的寂静和无形的黑暗弄得我神经紧绷，耳边三英寸处一个平静的声音说话时，我猛地一惊。

「站住！什么人？」

是个法国哨兵，背抵着屋墙站在那样一口黑的深潭里，连刺刀也不见一线光。

战争的又一天来了。世界古老的美还在，紧挨着那些古铜色麦田的线——泼着罂粟的猩红和新割麦捆的淡黄，一直延伸过去，没有一道树篱的间断，直到接天的最后几道坡。

---

我站在那些收获的田里，瞪望一道隆起的高坡，那里没有成熟的麦，连草也忽然停住，仿佛怕着什么。我知道其中缘故，也知道向两边各延出几英里的长长的白色土线是什么。那是德国战壕的胸墙，胸墙下的沟里是穴居人，拿着致命的武器，瞪过法兰西的美，或许纳闷自己为什么在这里精蹋它，同时盯着我——他们视野里的一个小黑点——悠闲地想着，放一颗子弹结束我的散步值不值。他们轻易办得到，可懒得费事。没有枪声或炮弹来穿透蜜蜂的嗡嗡，或砸穿风的叹息——风正弯下所有的麦穗，去听法兰西这些田野里絮语的虫声。

离我不远是一群庄稼人——米勒那样的画家的一幅画。其中一个朝我喊：「Voilà les Boches（瞧那些德国佬）！」朝左右挥着胳膊，又朝他们晃一只攥紧的拳头。

===Original===

A sturdy girl with a brown throat showing through an open bodice munched an apple, like Audrey in *As You Like It*, and between her bites told me that she had had a brother killed in the war, and that she had been nearly killed herself, a week ago, by shells that came bursting all round her as she was tying up her sheaves (she pointed to great holes in the field), and described the coming of the Germans into her village over there, when she had lied to some Uhlans about the whereabouts of French soldiers and had given one of those fat Germans a blow on the face when he had tried to make love to her in her father’s barn. Her mother had been raped.

In further fields out of view of the German trenches, but well within shell-range, the harvesting was being done by French soldiers. One of them was driving the reaping-machine and looked like a gunner on his limber, with his képi thrust to the back of his head. The trousers of his comrades were as red as the poppies that grew on the edge of the wheat, and three of these poilus had ceased their work to drink out of a leather wine-bottle which had been replenished from a handcart. It was a pretty scene if one could forget the grim purpose which had put those harvesters in uniform.

The same thought was in the mind of a British officer.

“A beautiful country, this,” he said. “It’s a pity to cut it up with trenches and barbed wire.”

Battalions of New Army men were being reviewed but a furlong or two away from that Invisible Man who was wielding a scythe which had no mercy for unripe wheat. Out of those lines of eyes stared the courage of men’s souls, not shirking the next ordeal.

It was through red ears of corn, in that summer of ’15, that one found one’s way to many of the trenches that marked the boundary-lines of the year’s harvesting, and in Belgium (by Kemmel Hill) the shells of our batteries, answered by German guns, came with their long-drawn howls of murder across the heads of peasant women who were gleaning, with bent backs.

---

===Chinese===

一个结实的姑娘，敞开的衣领露出褐色的脖颈，嚼着一只苹果，像《皆大欢喜》里的奥德蕾，咬着咬着告诉我：她有个兄弟阵亡了；她自己一星期前差点被打死，捆麦捆时炮弹在她四周炸开（她指着田里的大坑）；还说德国人当时怎样进她那边的村子，她对几个枪骑兵撒了谎，不告诉他们法国兵的下落，一个胖德国人在她父亲的谷仓里想调戏她，她给了他脸上一拳。她母亲被强奸了。

更远的田里，德国战壕看不见、炮弹够得着的地方，收割由法国士兵在做。其中一个赶着割麦机，像坐在前车上的炮手，军帽推到后脑勺。他的战友们的裤子红得同麦田边的罂粟一样，三个大兵停下活，对着一只从手推车里续过酒的皮酒囊喝酒。要是能忘掉把这些收割人塞进军装的那个冷酷目的，这景象是美的。

同一个念头也在一位英国军官心里。

「好一个美的国家，」他说。「拿战壕和铁丝网把它裁开，可惜了。」

新军的几个营正在受阅，离那位挥着对青麦毫不留情的镰刀的看不见的人，只有一两浪远。那一片片目光里瞪出来的是人灵魂的勇气，不躲避下一场煎熬。

一九一五年那个夏天，人是沿着红麦穗找到路，走进那些标志着当年收获边界线的战壕的；在比利时（凯梅尔山边），我们炮兵连的炮弹与德军的炮火应答着，拖着长长的凶杀的嚎，越过弯着腰拾穗的农妇头顶。

---

===Original===

In Plug Street Wood the trees had worn thin under showers of shrapnel, but the long avenues between the trenches were cool and pleasant in the heat of the day. It was one of the elementary schools where many of our soldiers learned the A.B.C. of actual warfare after their training in camps behind the lines. Here one might sport with Amaryllis in the shade, but for the fact that country wenches were not allowed in the dugouts and trenches, where I found our soldiers killing flies in the intervals between potshots at German periscopes.

The enemy was engaged, presumably, in the same pursuit of killing time and life (with luck), and sniping was hot on both sides, so that the wood resounded with sharp reports as though hard filbert nuts were being cracked by giant teeth. Each time I went there one of our men was hit by a sniper, and his body was carried off for burial as I went toward the first line of trenches, hoping that my shadow would not fall across a German periscope. The sight of that dead body passing chilled one a little. There were many graves in the bosky arbors﻿—eighteen under one mound﻿—but some of those who had fallen six months before still lay where the gleaners could not reach them.

I used to peer through the leaves of Plug Street Wood at No Man’s Land between the lines, where every creature had been killed by the sweeping flail of machine-guns and shrapnel. Along the harvest-fields there were many barren territories like that, and up by Hooge, along the edge of the fatal crater, and behind the stripped trees of Zouave Wood there was no other gleaning to be had but that of broken shells and shrapnel bullets and a litter of limbs.

===Chinese===

普卢格街林子里，树被雹弹雨削瘦了，可战壕间的长长的林荫道在白天暑热里凉爽宜人。那是许多士兵在后方营地训练之后学习实战入门的一所所小学之一。在这里本可以在树荫下同阿玛丽利斯调情——若不是村姑不许进地洞和战壕的话；我就在那些地方看见我们的士兵在朝德国潜望镜打冷枪的间隙里拍苍蝇。

敌人想必也在干同样的杀时间（碰运气杀生命）的营生，两边狙击都热，林子里脆响不断，像巨人的牙在磕硬榛子。我每回去，都有一个我们的人挨狙击手的枪，我朝一线战壕走、巴望自己的影子别落上一架德国潜望镜时，那具尸体正被抬去下葬。死尸抬过的一瞥叫人心里一凉。林荫深处有许多坟——一个土丘下十八座——可半年前倒下的有些人，还躺在拾穗人够不着的地方。

我常透过普卢格街林的树叶窥看两线之间的无人区，那里一切生灵都被机枪和雹弹的连枷扫尽。沿着收获的田野，这样的荒地很多，胡格上边、致命爆破坑的边沿、祖阿夫林剥光的树后面，能拾的只有碎弹壳、雹弹丸，和一地残肢。

### XV / 十五

### XV / 
===Original===

For some time the War Office would not allow military bands at the front, not understanding that music was like water to parched souls. By degrees divisional generals realized the utter need of entertainment among men dulled and dazed by the routine of war, and encouraged “variety” shows, organized by young officers who had been amateur actors before the war, who searched around for likely talent. There was plenty of it in the New Army, including professional “funny men,” trick cyclists, conjurers, and singers of all kinds. So by the summer of ’15 most of the divisions had their dramatic entertainments: “The Follies,” “The Bow Bells,” “The Jocks,” “The Pip-Squeaks,” “The Whizzbangs,” “The Diamonds,” “The Brass Hats,” “The Verey Lights,” and many others with fancy names.

I remember going to one of the first of them in the village of Acheux, a few miles from the German lines. It was held in an old sugar-factory, and I shall long remember the impressions of the place, with seven or eight hundred men sitting in the gloom of that big, broken, barn-like building, where strange bits of machinery looked through the darkness, and where through gashes in the walls stars twinkled.

There was a smell of clay and moist sugar and tarpaulins and damp khaki, and chloride of lime, very pungent in one’s nostrils, and when the curtain went up on a well-fitted stage and “The Follies” began their performance, the squalor of the place did not matter. What mattered was the enormous whimsicality of the Bombardier at the piano, and the outrageous comicality of a tousle-haired soldier with a red nose, who described how he had run away from Mons “with the rest of you,” and the lightheartedness of a performance which could have gone straight to a London music-hall and brought down the house with jokes and songs made up in dugouts and front-line trenches.

===Chinese===

有段时间陆军部不许军乐队上前线，不明白音乐对干渴的灵魂如水。师长们渐渐明白被战争的例行公事磨钝、震昏的人对娱乐的绝顶需要，鼓励起「杂耍」演出，由战前做过业余演员的年轻军官组织，四下搜罗人才。新军里人才多的是，包括职业「滑稽人」、车技杂耍师、魔术师，各路歌手。于是到一九一五年夏天，多数师有了自己的戏剧演出：「活宝」「钟声」「苏格兰佬」「小尖叫」「嗖嗖弹」「钻石」「铜帽子」「信号光」，还有许多花哨名字。

我记得去阿舍村看了最早几场之一，离德军防线几英里。演出在一座旧糖厂里，那地方的印象我会久记：七八百人坐在那大而破败、谷仓似的建筑的昏暗里，古怪的机器残件从黑暗里张望，墙上的裂口外星星眨眼。

那里有黏土、潮糖、油布、湿卡其布和漂白粉的气味，冲鼻得很；可幕布在一座像模像样的舞台上升起、「活宝」开演之后，地方的腌臜不要紧了。要紧的是那位弹钢琴的炮兵下士天大的谐趣，是一个红鼻子的乱发士兵的放肆的滑稽——他讲他怎么从蒙斯「同你们大伙一起」跑回来的——还有整场演出的轻快，它可以径直搬上伦敦音乐厅，用地洞里、一线战壕里编出来的笑话和歌赢个满堂彩。

===Original===

At first the audience sat silent, with glazed eyes. It was difficult to get a laugh out of them. The mud of the trenches was still on them. They stank of the trenches, and the stench was in their souls. Presently they began to brighten up. Life came back into their eyes. They laughed!﻿ ﻿… Later, from this audience of soldiers there were yells of laughter, though the effect of shells arriving at unexpected moments, in untoward circumstances, was a favorite theme of the jesters. Many of the men were going into the trenches that night again, and there would be no fun in the noise of the shells, but they went more gaily and with stronger hearts, I am sure, because of the laughter which had roared through the old sugar-factory.

A night or two later I went to another concert and heard the same gaiety of men who had been through a year of war. It was in an open field, under a velvety sky studded with innumerable stars. Nearly a thousand soldiers trooped through the gates and massed before the little canvas theater. In front a small crowd of Flemish children squatted on the grass, not understanding a word of the jokes, but laughing in shrill delight at the antics of soldier-Pierrots. The corner-man was a funny fellow, and his byplay with a stout Flemish woman round the flap of the canvas screen, to whom he made amorous advances while his comrades were singing sentimental ballads, was truly comic. The hit of the evening was when an Australian behind the stage gave an unexpected imitation of a laughing-jackass.

There was something indescribably weird and wild and grotesque in that prolonged cry of cackling, unnatural mirth. An Australian by my side said: “Well done! Exactly right!” and the Flemish children shrieked with joy, without understanding the meaning of the noise. Old, old songs belonging to the early Victorian age were given by the soldiers, who had great emotion and broke down sometimes in the middle of a verse. There were funny men dressed in the Widow Twankey style, or in burlesque uniforms, who were greeted with yells of laughter by their comrades. An Australian giant played some clever card tricks, and another Australian recited Kipling’s “Gunga Din” with splendid fire. And between every “turn” the soldiers in the field roared out a chorus:

“Jolly good song,

Jolly well sung.

If you can think of a better you’re welcome to try.

===Chinese===

起初观众默默地坐着眼发直。逗他们笑不容易。战壕的泥还挂在身上。他们身上有战壕的臭，那臭进了灵魂。渐渐地他们亮起来。生命回到眼睛里。他们笑了！……后来，这群士兵观众爆出大笑，虽然炮弹在不巧的时辰、不巧的场合突然驾到，正是小丑们最爱的题目。许多人当夜又要进战壕，炮弹的响声里没有好玩，可他们走得更欢、心更壮，我确信，因为那阵笑吼过旧糖厂。

一两天后的夜里我又去了一场音乐会，听见了经历过一年战争的人同样的快活。那是在一片露天野地里，天鹅绒的天空缀满星。近千名士兵鱼贯进门，聚在小小的帆布戏台前。前排一小群佛兰德斯孩子蹲在草上，笑话一个词听不懂，却冲着士兵丑角的滑稽尖声大笑。角落里那人是把好手，他隔着帆布屏的掀缝同一位壮实的佛兰德斯大娘的插科打诨真逗——同伴们正唱伤感的叙事歌，他却向她大献殷勤。当晚最出彩的，是台后一个澳大利亚人出其不意学了一声笑翠鸟。

那阵咯咯的、非自然的欢畅长鸣，有种说不出的怪诞、野性和荒唐。我身边的一个澳大利亚人说：「学得好！一模一样！」佛兰德斯孩子们欢叫，全不懂那声音的意思。士兵们唱着早维多利亚时代的老歌，唱得动了情，有时唱到半节唱不下去。有打扮成特温基寡妇式样、或穿滑稽军装的丑角，惹得战友们哄叫。一个澳大利亚大个儿变了几手漂亮的牌戏，另一个澳大利亚人朗诵吉卜林的《雍迦丁》，火气十足。而在每个节目之间，场子里的士兵们齐吼一段副歌：

「好歌，

唱得真好。

你要能想出更好的，欢迎来试。

===Original===

But don’t forget the singer is dry;

Give the poor beggar some beer!”

A touring company of mouth-organ musicians was having a great success in the war zone. But, apart from all those organized methods of mirth, there was a funny man in every billet who played the part of court jester, and clowned it whatever the state of the weather or the risks of war. The British soldier would have his game of “house” or “crown and anchor” even on the edge of the shell-storm, and his little bit of sport wherever there was room to stretch his legs. It was a jesting army (though some of its jokes were very grim), and those who saw, as I did, the daily tragedy of war, never ceasing, always adding to the sum of human suffering, were not likely to discourage that sense of humor.

---

A successful concert with mouth-organs, combs, and tissue-paper and penny whistles was given by the Guards in the front-line trenches near Loos. They played old English melodies, harmonized with great emotion and technical skill. It attracted an unexpected audience. The Germans crowded into their front line﻿—not far away﻿—and applauded each number. Presently, in good English, a German voice shouted across:

“Play ‘Annie Laurie’ and I will sing it.”

The Guards played “Annie Laurie,” and a German officer stood up on the parapet﻿—the evening sun was red behind him﻿—and sang the old song admirably, with great tenderness. There was applause on both sides.

“Let’s have another concert tomorrow!” shouted the Germans.

But there was a different kind of concert next day, and the music was played by trench-mortars, Mills bombs, rifle-grenades, and other instruments of death in possession of the Guards. There were cries of agony and terror from the German trenches, and young officers of the Guards told the story as an amusing anecdote, with loud laughter.

===Chinese===

可别忘了唱歌的口渴；

给这可怜虫来点啤酒！」

一支巡回的口琴乐队正在战区大走红。但除了这些有组织的欢乐，每个驻地都有自己的丑角，扮演宫廷弄臣，无论天时不天时、冒险不冒险都插科打诨。英国士兵哪怕在炮风暴的边上也要玩他的「房子」或「王冠锚」，有一块伸腿的地方就要来一点他的小竞技。这是一支爱说笑的军队（虽然有些笑话冷得很），凡像我这样天天看着战争的悲剧——它从不间断，一直往人类苦难的总数上添加——的人，都不会去挫伤那种幽默感。

---

近卫团在鲁斯近旁的一线战壕里，用口琴、梳子和绵纸、便士哨开了一场成功的音乐会。他们演奏古老的英格兰旋律，和声带着深情和技巧。它引来了一群意料之外的听众。德国人挤进了他们的一线——不远——每个曲子都鼓掌。过了一会儿，一个德国声音用漂亮的英语隔空喊：

「奏《安妮·劳丽》，我来唱。」

近卫兵奏起《安妮·劳丽》，一个德国军官站上胸墙——晚霞在他身后红着——唱起那支老歌，唱得极好，深情极了。两边都鼓了掌。

「明天再开一场音乐会吧！」德国人喊。

可第二天是另一种音乐会，乐曲由迫击炮、米尔斯手榴弹、枪榴弹，和近卫团手中的别的死亡乐器演奏。德国战壕里传出痛苦和恐怖的叫喊，近卫团的年轻军官们把这事当逗乐的轶事讲，讲时哈哈大笑。

### XVI / 十六
===Original===

It was astonishing how loudly one laughed at tales of gruesome things, of war’s brutality﻿—I with the rest of them. I think at the bottom of it was a sense of the ironical contrast between the normal ways of civilian life and this hark-back to the caveman code. It made all our old philosophy of life monstrously ridiculous. It played the “hat trick” with the gentility of modern manners. Men who had been brought up to Christian virtues, who had prattled their little prayers at mothers’ knees, who had grown up to a love of poetry, painting, music, the gentle arts, over-sensitized to the subtleties of halftones, delicate scales of emotion, fastidious in their choice of words, in their sense of beauty, found themselves compelled to live and act like ape-men; and it was abominably funny. They laughed at the most frightful episodes, which revealed this contrast between civilized ethics and the old beast law. The more revolting it was the more, sometimes, they shouted with laughter, especially in reminiscence, when the tale was told in the gilded salon of a French château, or at a mess-table.

It was, I think, the laughter of mortals at the trick which had been played on them by an ironical fate. They had been taught to believe that the whole object of life was to reach out to beauty and love, and that mankind, in its progress to perfection, had killed the beast instinct, cruelty, bloodlust, the primitive, savage law of survival by tooth and claw and club and ax. All poetry, all art, all religion had preached this gospel and this promise.

Now that ideal had broken like a china vase dashed to hard ground. The contrast between That and This was devastating. It was, in an enormous world-shaking way, like a highly dignified man in a silk hat, morning coat, creased trousers, spats, and patent boots suddenly slipping on a piece of orange-peel and sitting, all of a heap, with silk hat flying, in a filthy gutter. The wartime humor of the soul roared with mirth at the sight of all that dignity and elegance despoiled.

===Chinese===

人对可怕的事情、战争的残暴的传闻，笑得多么响——我也同他们一起笑。我想根子上是一种感觉：平民生活的正常方式同这穴居人法典的回返之间那讥诮的反差。它把我们整套旧的人生哲学弄得荒唐透顶。它把现代举止的体面来了个「帽子戏法」。那些从小受基督教美德教养、在母亲膝边咿呀学祷、长大后爱上诗歌绘画音乐温柔艺术、对半音调的微妙和情感的细梯度过敏、在选词和美感上挑剔的人，发现自己被迫像猿人一样生活和行动；而这是天大的滑稽。他们笑最骇人的情节，那些显出文明伦理同老兽律反差的情节。越可怖，有时他们笑得越响，尤其是事后追忆的时候，故事在法兰西城堡的镀金客厅里、在食堂餐桌上讲出来。

我想，那是必死者对遭到反讽命运捉弄的笑。他们受的教育说，人生的全部目的是伸手够向美与爱；人类在走向完善的路上，已经杀死了兽性本能、残忍、嗜血、那靠爪与牙、棍与斧生存的原始野蛮法则。一切诗歌、一切艺术、一切宗教都宣讲过这个福音和这个许诺。

如今那个理想摔碎了，像瓷瓶砸上硬地。「彼」与「此」的反差是毁灭性的。以一种撼动世界的巨大方式，它像一位极体面的先生——丝礼帽、晨礼服、笔挺的裤线、鞋罩、漆皮鞋——踩上一块橘子皮突然滑倒，一屁股坐进肮脏的阴沟，礼帽飞出去。战时灵魂的幽默望着那全部体面与优雅被精蹋的景象，轰然大笑。

===Original===

So we laughed merrily, I remember, when a military chaplain (Eton, Christ Church, and Christian service) described how an English sergeant stood round the traverse of a German trench, in a night raid, and as the Germans came his way, thinking to escape, he cleft one skull after another with a steel-studded bludgeon﻿—a weapon which he had made with loving craftsmanship on the model of Blunderbore’s club in the pictures of a fairytale.

So we laughed at the adventures of a young barrister (a brilliant fellow in the Oxford “Union”) whose pleasure it was to creep out o’ nights into No Man’s Land and lie doggo in a shell-hole close to the enemy’s barbed wire, until presently, after an hour’s waiting or two, a German soldier would crawl out to fetch in a corpse. The English barrister lay with his rifle ready. Where there had been one corpse there were two. Each night he made a notch on his rifle﻿—three notches one night﻿—to check the number of his victims. Then he came back to breakfast in his dugout with a hearty appetite.

---

In one section of trenches the men made a habit of betting upon those who would be wounded first. It had all the uncertainty of the roulette-table﻿ ﻿… One day, when the German gunners were putting over a special dose of hate, a sergeant kept coming to one dugout to inquire about a “new chum,” who had come up with the drafts.

“Is Private Smith all right?” he asked.

“Yes, Sergeant, he’s all right,” answered the men crouching in the dark hole.

“Private Smith isn’t wounded yet?” asked the, sergeant again, five minutes later.

“No, Sergeant.”

Private Smith was touched by this interest in his well-being.

“That sergeant seems a very kind man,” said the boy. “Seems to love me like a father!”

A yell of laughter answered him.

“You poor, bleeding fool!” said one of his comrades. “He’s drawn you in a lottery! Stood to win if you’d been hit.”

---

In digging new trenches and new dugouts, bodies and bits of bodies were unearthed, and put into sandbags with the soil that was sent back down a line of men concealing their work from German eyes waiting for any new activity in our ditches.

“Bit of Bill,” said the leading man, putting in a leg.

“Another bit of Bill,” he said, unearthing a hand.

“Bill’s ugly mug,” he said at a later stage in the operations, when a head was found.

===Chinese===

于是我们快活地笑了，我记得，当一位随军牧师（伊顿、基督堂、基督事工）讲起，一个英国军士在夜袭里守在德国战壕一个掩体的拐角，德国人朝他这边逃过来时，他用一根钉钢的短棒一个接一个劈开他们的脑壳——那武器是他照童话画里巨人布伦德博的大棒精心打造的。

我们还笑一位年轻出庭律师（牛津「联合会」的出色人物）的奇遇：他的乐趣是夜里爬进无人区，趴在敌人铁丝网近旁的弹坑里装死，等上一两个钟头，总有一个德国兵爬出来收尸。英国律师端着枪等。原先一具尸体的地方成了两具。他每夜在枪托上刻一道——有一夜刻了三道——记他的猎物数。然后回地洞里吃早饭，胃口极好。

---

有一段战壕里，士兵们养成了赌谁先挂彩的习惯。那有轮盘赌的全部变数……一天，德国炮兵正下特别大剂量的「恨」，一个军士一趟趟跑到一个地洞来打听一个「新伙计」——随补充兵上来的。

「史密斯列兵没事吧？」他问。

「没事，军士，他好着呢，」蹲在黑洞里的人答。

「史密斯列兵还没挂彩？」五分钟后军士又问。

「没有，军士。」

史密斯列兵被这份关怀感动了。

「那军士真是个好人，」男孩说。「疼我疼得像亲爹！」

回答他的是一片大笑。

「你这个可怜的傻蛋！」一个战友说。「他把你抽进赌局了！你要挨了打他就能赢钱。」

---

挖新战壕新地洞的时候，尸体和碎尸被翻出来，连同土一起装进沙袋，沿一列人传到后面——大家藏着活，不让守着我们壕沟新动静的德国眼睛看见。

「比尔的一块，」排头的人说，放进一条腿。

「比尔的又一块，」他翻出一只手时说。

「比尔的丑脸，」工程后段挖出一颗头时他说。

===Original===

As told afterward, that little episode in the trenches seemed immensely comic. Generals chuckled over it. Chaplains treasured it.

---

How we used to guffaw at the answer of the cockney soldier who met a German soldier with his hands up, crying: “Kamerad! Kamerad! Mercy!”

“Not so much of your ‘Mercy, Kamerad,’ ” said the cockney. “ ’And us over your bloody ticker!”

It was the man’s watch he wanted, without sentiment.

---

One tale was most popular, most mirth-arousing in the early days of the war.

“Where’s your prisoner?” asked an Intelligence officer waiting to receive a German sent down from the trenches under escort of an honest corporal.

“I lost him on the way, sir,” said the corporal.

“Lost him?”

The corporal was embarrassed.

“Very sorry, sir. My feelings overcame me, sir. It was like this, sir. The man started talking on the way down. Said he was thinking of his poor wife. I’d been thinking of mine, and I felt sorry for him. Then he mentioned as how he had two kiddies at home. I ’ave two kiddies at ’ome, sir, and I couldn’t ’elp feeling sorry for him. Then he said as how his old mother had died awhile ago and he’d never see her again. When he started cryin’ I was so sorry for him I couldn’t stand it any longer, sir. So I killed the poor blighter.”

---

Our men in the trenches, and out of them, up to the waist in water sometimes, lying in slimy dugouts, lice-eaten, rat-haunted, on the edge of mine-craters, under harassing fire, with just the fluke of luck between life and death, seized upon any kind of joke as an excuse for laughter, and many a time in ruins and in trenches and in dugouts I have heard great laughter. It was the protective armor of men’s souls. They knew that if they did not laugh their courage would go and nothing would stand between them and fear.

“You know, sir,” said a sergeant-major, one day, when I walked with him down a communication trench so waterlogged that my top-boots were full of slime, “it doesn’t do to take this war seriously.”

And, as though in answer to him, a soldier without breeches and with his shirt tied between his legs looked at me and remarked, in a philosophical way, with just a glint of comedy in his eyes:

“That there Grand Fleet of ours don’t seem to be very active, sir. It’s a pity it don’t come down these blinkin’ trenches and do a bit of work!”

---

===Chinese===

事后讲起来，战壕里这段小插曲显得无比滑稽。将军们听了偷笑。牧师们珍藏它。

---

我们从前怎样哄笑那个伦敦士兵的回答啊——他碰上一个举着双手的德国兵，德国兵喊着：「Kamerad！Kamerad！Mercy（战友！战友！饶命）！」

「少来你那套『饶命，战友』，」伦敦佬说。「把你那该死的表交出来！」

他要的是那人的手表，不带一点感情。

---

有一个故事战争早期最流行、最逗乐。

「你的俘虏呢？」一位情报军官问，他等着接收一个由老实下士从战壕押下来的德国兵。

「路上把他丢了，长官，」下士说。

「丢了？」

下士很窘。

「非常抱歉，长官。我感情用事了，长官。是这样的，长官。那人在路上开了口。说他想他可怜的老婆。我也一直在想我的，就替他难受。后来他又说家里有两个小家伙。俺家也有两个小家伙，长官，俺没法不替他难受。后来他又说他老娘前一阵死了，他再也见不着了。他一哭，俺替他难受得受不了啦，长官。所以俺把那可怜虫宰了。」

---

我们在战壕里的、在战壕外的士兵——有时水齐腰，躺着黏滑的地洞，虱咬鼠扰，爆破坑边，袭扰炮火下，生死之间只隔一阵运气的偶然——抓住任何一种玩笑作笑的理由，多少次，在废墟里、战壕里、地洞里，我听见巨大的笑声。那是人灵魂的护甲。他们知道，不笑，勇气就没了，他们同恐惧之间就什么也不剩了。

「您知道，长官，」一天，一位军士长同我走在一条积水没靴、灌满烂泥的交通壕里时说，「这场战争，当真不得。」

像是答他，一个没穿马裤、衬衣在裆间打了结的士兵看着我，哲学似的说，眼里带一线滑稽：

「咱们那大舰队好像不大来劲儿啊，长官。可惜它不下到这些破战壕里干点活！」

---

===Original===

“Having a cleanup, my man?” said a brigadier to a soldier trying to wash in a basin about the size of a kitchen mug.

“Yes, sir,” said the man, “and I wish I was a blasted canary.”

---

One of the most remarkable battles on the front was fought by a battalion of Worcesters for the benefit of two English members of Parliament. It was not a very big battle, but most dramatic while it lasted. The colonel (who had a sense of humor) arranged it after a telephone message to his dugout telling him that two politicians were about to visit his battalion in the line, and asking him to show them something interesting.

“Interesting?” said the colonel. “Do they think this war is a peepshow for politicians? Do they want me to arrange a massacre to make a London holiday?” Then his voice changed and he laughed. “Show them something interesting? Oh, all right; I dare say I can do that.”

He did. When the two M.P.’s arrived, apparently at the front-line trenches, they were informed by the colonel that, much to his regret, for their sake, the enemy was just attacking, and that his men were defending their position desperately.

“We hope for the best,” he said, “and I think there is just a chance that you will escape with your lives if you stay here quite quietly.”

“Great God!” said one of the M.P.’s, and the other was silent, but pale.

Certainly there was all the noise of a big attack. The Worcesters were standing-to on the fire-step, firing rifle-grenades and throwing bombs with terrific energy. Every now and then a man fell, and the stretcher-bearers pounced on him, tied him up in bandages, and carried him away to the field dressing-station, whistling as they went, “We won’t go home till morning,” in a most heroic way﻿ ﻿… The battle lasted twenty minutes, at the end of which time the colonel announced to his visitors:

“The attack is repulsed, and you, gentlemen, have nothing more to fear.”

One of the M.P.’s was thrilled with excitement. “The valor of your men was marvelous,” he said. “What impressed me most was the cheerfulness of the wounded. They were actually grinning as they came down on the stretchers.”

The colonel grinned, too. In fact, he stifled a fit of coughing. “Funny devils!” he said. “They are so glad to be going home.”

===Chinese===

「大扫除呢，老弟？」一位旅长对一个正想在一只厨房水杯大小的盆里洗漱的士兵说。

「是，长官，」那人说，「我真恨不得自己是只金丝雀。」

---

前线最出色的一场战斗之一，是伍斯特郡营为两位英国下院议员演的。仗不大，进行时却极有戏。上校（有幽默感）在接到地洞里那通电话后安排了它——电话说两位政客要来他前线上的营，请他给他们看点有意思的东西。

「有意思？」上校说。「他们当这战争是给政客看的西洋景？要我安排一场屠杀作伦敦的节日？」随后他口气一转，笑了。「看点有意思的？哦，行；我想我办得到。」

他办到了。两位议员到了——看样子是一线战壕——上校告诉他们，非常遗憾，为了他们，敌人恰好正在进攻，他的部下正拼命守着阵地。

「我们抱最好的希望，」他说，「我想，只要你们待在这儿安安静静，还是有一线机会活着出去的。」

「老天爷！」一位议员说，另一位没作声，脸白了。

确实有大攻击的全套响动。伍斯特郡兵站在射击踏垛上，凶猛地放枪榴弹、扔手榴弹。不时有人倒下，担架手扑上去，用绷带把他扎好，抬去前方包扎站，一路吹着《不到早晨不回家》，一副英雄气概……战斗持续了二十分钟，末了上校向客人宣布：

「进攻已被击退，诸位先生没有什么可怕的了。」

一位议员激动坏了。「您部下的英勇了不起，」他说。「最打动我的是伤员的快活。他们抬下来的时候居然还咧着嘴笑。」

上校也咧嘴。其实他忍住了一阵咳嗽。「滑稽鬼！」他说。「回家去，他们高兴着呢。」

===Original===

The members of Parliament went away enormously impressed, but they had not enjoyed themselves nearly as well as the Worcesters, who had fought a sham battle﻿—not in the front-line trenches, but in the support trenches two miles back! They laughed for a week afterward.

===Chinese===

议员们带着极深的印象走了，可他们到底不如伍斯特郡兵玩得痛快——那是一场假仗，不在一线战壕，而在两英里后的支援壕里！他们后来笑了一个星期。

### XVII / 十七
===Original===

On the hill at Wizerne, not far from the stately old town of St.-Omer (visited from time to time by monstrous night-birds who dropped high-explosive eggs), was a large convent. There were no nuns there, but generally some hundreds of young officers and men from many different battalions, attending a machine-gun course under the direction of General Baker-Carr, who was the master machine-gunner of the British army (at a time when we were very weak in those weapons compared with the enemy’s strength) and a cheery, vital man.

“This war has produced two great dugouts,” said Lord Kitchener on a visit to the convent. “Me and Baker-Carr.”

It was the boys who interested me more than the machines. (I was never much interested in the machinery of war.) They came down from the trenches to this school with a sense of escape from prison, and for the ten days of their course they were like “freshers” at Oxford and made the most of their minutes, organizing concerts and other entertainments in the evenings after their initiation into the mysteries of Vickers and Lewis. I was invited to dinner there one night, and sat between two young cavalry officers on long benches crowded with subalterns of many regiments. It was a merry meal and a good one﻿—to this day I remember a potato pie, gloriously baked, and afterward, as it was the last night of the course, all the officers went wild and indulged in a “rag” of the public-school kind. They straddled across the benches and barged at each other in single tourneys and jousts, riding their hobbyhorses with violent rearings and plungings and bruising one another without grievous hurt and with yells of laughter. Glasses broke, crockery crashed upon the polished boards. One boy danced the Highland fling on the tables, others were waltzing down the corridors. There was a Rugby scrum in the refectory, and hunting-men cried the “View halloo!” and shouted “Yoicks! yoicks!”﻿ ﻿… General Baker-Carr was a human soul, and kept to his own room that night and let discipline go hang.﻿ ﻿…

===Chinese===

维泽讷山上——离庄严的老城圣奥梅尔不远（那城不时被投高爆蛋的怪物夜鸟光顾）——有一座大修道院。里面没有修女，倒通常有几百名来自各营的年轻军官和士兵，在贝克-卡尔将军主持下上机枪课。贝克-卡尔将军是英军的机枪宗师（其时我们在这种武器上同敌人相比还很弱），也是个快活而元气充沛的人。

「这场战争造就了两个大地洞，」基奇纳勋爵视察修道院时说。「我和贝克-卡尔。」

比机器更让我感兴趣的是那些男孩。（战争的机器我从来不大感兴趣。）他们从战壕下到这所学校，带着越狱的感觉，课程十天里他们像牛津的「新鲜人」，把每一分钟用到头，白天学维克斯和刘易斯的奥秘，晚上组织音乐会和别的娱乐。一天晚上我被请去吃饭，坐在两位年轻骑兵军官中间，长凳上挤满各团的少尉。那是一顿热闹的好饭——至今我还记得一个土豆派，烤得辉煌——饭后，因为是课程最后一夜，全体军官撒起野来，玩起公学式的「闹堂」。他们跨坐在长凳上，单打独斗地互相撞，骑着想象的木马猛烈地人立、俯冲，把彼此撞得生疼却无重伤，喊笑连天。杯子碎了，陶器砸在亮地板上。一个男孩在桌上跳高地舞，另一些在走廊里跳华尔兹。饭堂里来了一场橄榄球集团对抗，打猎的人们喊着「见猎欢呼！」，大叫「嗬咿！嗬咿！」……贝克-卡尔将军是个通人性的人，那晚守在自己屋里，由纪律见鬼去。……

===Original===

When the battles of the Somme began it was those young officers who led their machine-gun sections into the woods of death﻿—Belville Wood, Mametz Wood, High Wood, and the others. It was they who afterward held the outpost lines in Flanders. Some of them were still alive on March 21, 1918, when they were surrounded by a sea of Germans and fought until the last, in isolated redoubts north and south of St.-Quentin. Two of them are still alive, those between whom I sat at dinner that night, and who escaped many close calls of death before the armistice. Of the others who charged one another with wooden benches, their laughter ringing out, some were blown to bits, and some were buried alive, and some were blinded and gassed, and some went “missing” forevermore.

===Chinese===

索姆河各战役打响时，正是这些年轻军官带着他们的机枪组开进死亡的树林——贝尔维尔林、马梅茨林、高林，和其他。后来在佛兰德斯据守前哨线的也是他们。有些人活到一九一八年三月二十一日，在圣康南北两面的孤立堡垒里陷进德国人的海洋，战斗到最后。他们中的两个今天还活着——那晚吃饭我坐在他们俩中间，停战前他们多次与死亡擦肩。其余那些跨着木凳互相冲锋、笑声朗朗的人，有的被炸成碎块，有的被活埋，有的瞎了眼中了毒气，有的从此「失踪」，永远。

### XVIII / 十八
===Original===

In those long days of trench warfare and stationary lines it was boredom that was the worst malady of the mind; a large, overwhelming boredom to thousands of men who were in exile from the normal interests of life and from the activities of brain-work; an intolerable, abominable boredom, sapping the willpower, the moral code, the intellect; a boredom from which there seemed no escape except by death, no relief except by vice, no probable or possible change in its dreary routine. It was bad enough in the trenches, where men looked across the parapet to the same corner of hell day by day, to the same dead bodies rotting by the edge of the same mine-crater, to the same old sandbags in the enemy’s line, to the blasted tree sliced by shellfire, the upturned railway-truck of which only the metal remained, the distant fringe of trees like gallows on the skyline, the broken spire of a church which could be seen in the round O of the telescope when the weather was not too misty. In “quiet” sections of the line the only variation to the routine was the number of casualties day by day, by casual shellfire or snipers’ bullets, and that became part of the boredom. “What casualties?” asked the adjutant in his dugout.

“Two killed, three wounded, sir.”

“Very well﻿ ﻿… You can go.”

A salute in the doorway of the dugout, a groan from the adjutant lighting another cigarette, leaning with his elbow on the deal table, staring at the guttering of the candle by his side, at the pile of forms in front of him, at the glint of light on the steel helmet hanging by its strap on a nail near the shelf where he kept his safety-razor, flash-lamp, love-letters (in an old cigar-box), soap, whisky-bottle (almost empty now), and an unread novel.

“Hell!﻿ ﻿… What a life!”

But there was always work to do, and odd incidents, and frights, and responsibilities.

===Chinese===

在阵地战和固定战线的漫长日子里，无聊是心灵最坏的病；对成千上万被放逐出生活的正常兴致和脑力活动之外的人，是一种浩大的、压倒的无聊；一种难堪的、可憎的无聊，蛀蚀意志、道德和智力；一种除了死似乎无路可逃、除了堕落无以缓解、阴沉的例规里无可期待也无可改变的无聊。在战壕里已够坏了——人们日复一日隔着胸墙望着同一个地狱的角落，望着同一具尸体在同一个爆破坑边腐烂，望着敌线上同一批旧沙袋，望着被炮火剖开的枯树、只剩铁皮的翻倒车皮、天边绞架似的一线树影、天气不太雾时从望远镜圆圈里望得见的教堂断塔。在「安静」地段，例规的唯一变化是一天的伤亡数字——零星的炮火或狙击手的子弹——而那也成了无聊的一部分。「伤亡多少？」副官在地洞里问。

「亡二伤三，长官。」

「很好……去吧。」

地洞口一个敬礼，副官点起另一支烟的一声叹息，肘撑在松木桌上，瞪着身边蜡烛的淌泪，瞪着面前一摞表格，瞪着挂在钉子上晃的钢盔的反光——钉子在搁板近旁，搁板上放着他的保险剃刀、手电、情书（装在一只旧雪茄盒里）、肥皂、威士忌瓶（现在几乎空了），和一本没读的小说。

「地狱！……这叫什么日子！」

可总有活儿干，有意外的事，有惊吓，有责任。

===Original===

It was worse﻿—this boredom﻿—for men behind the lines; in lorry columns which went from railhead to dump every damned morning, and back again by the middle of the morning, and then nothing else to do for all the day, in a cramped little billet with a sulky woman in the kitchen, and squealing children in the yard, and a stench of manure through the small window. A dull life for an actor who had toured in England and America (like one I met dazed and stupefied by years of boredom﻿—paying too much for safety), or for a barrister who had many briefs before the war and now found his memory going, though a young man, because of the narrow limits of his life between one Flemish village and another, which was the length of his lorry column and of his adventure of war. Nothing ever happened to break the monotony﻿—not even shellfire. So it was also in small towns like Hesdin, St.-Pol, Bruay, Lillers﻿—a hundred others where officers stayed for years in charge of motor-repair shops, ordnance-stores, labor battalions, administration offices, claim commissions, graves’ registration, agriculture for soldiers, all kinds of jobs connected with that life of war, but not exciting.

Not exciting. So frightful in boredom that men were tempted to take to drink, to look around for unattached women, to gamble at cards with any poor devil like themselves. Those were most bored who were most virtuous. For them, with an ideal in their souls, there was no possibility of relief (for virtue is not its own reward), unless they were mystics, as some became, who found God good company and needed no other help. They had rare luck, those fellows with an astounding faith which rose above the irony and the brutality of that business being done in the trenches, but there were few of them.

===Chinese===

更坏——这无聊——对于战线后方的人；那些卡车队，每天该死的早晨从铁路终点站跑到堆栈，上午中段再跑回来，然后一整天没事可做，蜷在窄小的宿营地里，厨房一个愠怒的女人，院里尖叫的孩子，小窗灌进粪臭。对一个在英美巡演过的演员（像我遇见的一个那样——被经年的无聊震呆了——为安全付了太高的价），或者对一个战前案子多得接不完、如今发觉记性衰退的出庭律师——虽还年轻，因为他的生活就圈在一个佛兰德斯村到另一个村之间，那是他的卡车队的长度，也是他的战争的冒险的全部——这是沉闷的生活。什么都打不断这单调——连炮火也不。埃丹、圣波尔、布吕埃、利莱尔这些小镇也一样——还有一百个别处，军官们在那里一待几年，管着汽车修理所、军械库、劳工营、行政办公室、索赔委员会、坟墓登记、士兵农业，种种同战争生活相连却毫不刺激的差事。

不刺激。无聊得可怕，以致人们受诱惑去喝酒，去找不三不四的女人，去同自己一样的可怜虫赌牌。越有德的人越无聊。对他们——灵魂里有理想的人——没有缓解的可能（因为美德不是它自己的报酬），除非他们是神秘主义者——有些人成了——发现上帝是好伴，不需要别的帮助。那类人有稀罕的运气，那信仰惊人，超出了战壕里那桩事的讥诮与残暴；可他们寥寥无几。

===Original===

Even with hours of leisure, men who had been “bookish” could not read. That was a common phenomenon. I could read hardly at all, for years, and thousands were like me. The most “exciting” novel was dull stuff up against that world convulsion. What did the romance of love mean, the little tortures of one man’s heart, or one woman’s, troubled in their mating, when thousands of men were being killed and vast populations were in agony? History﻿—Greek or Roman or medieval﻿—what was the use of reading that old stuff, now that world history was being made with a rush? Poetry﻿—poor poets with their love of beauty! What did beauty matter, now that it lay dead in the soul of the world, under the filth of battlefields, and the dirt of hate and cruelty, and the law of the apelike man? No﻿—we could not read; but talked and talked about the old philosophy of life, and the structure of society, and Democracy and Liberty and Patriotism and Internationalism, and Brotherhood of Men, and God, and Christian ethics; and then talked no more, because all words were futile, and just brooded and brooded, after searching the daily paper (two days old) for any kind of hope and light, not finding either.

===Chinese===

即便有闲暇的钟点，从前「书卷气」的人也读不进书。那是普遍现象。我几年里几乎读不了任何东西，成千上万的人同我一样。最「刺激」的小说对着那场世界剧变也是钝物。当成千上万的人在死、庞大的种群在受难时，一个男人的心或一个女人的心在婚配上那点爱情的罗曼史、那点小苦楚，算什么？历史——希腊的罗马的中古的——世界史正哗哗地写，读那些老东西有什么用？诗——可怜的诗人们爱着美！美算什么，如今它死在世界的灵魂里，压在战场的污秽、仇恨与残暴的脏、猿人的法则底下。不——我们读不进；只是谈啊谈，谈旧的人生哲学、社会的结构、民主与自由与爱国主义与国际主义、人类手足、上帝、基督教伦理；然后不再谈了，因为一切言语无用，只是沉思复沉思，在两天前的日报里搜任何一点希望和光，什么也搜不到。

### XIX / 十九
===Original===

At first, in the beginning of the war, our officers and men believed that it would have a quick ending. Our first Expeditionary Force came out to France with the cheerful shout of “Now we shan’t be long!” before they fell back from an advancing tide of Germans from Mons to the Marne, and fell in their youth like autumn leaves. The New Army boys who followed them were desperate to get out to “the great adventure.” They cursed the length of their training in English camps. “We shan’t get out till it’s too late!” they said. Too late, O God! Even when they had had their first spell in the trenches and came up against German strength they kept a queer faith, for a time, that “something” would happen to bring peace as quickly as war had come. Peace was always coming three months ahead. Generals and staff-officers, as well as sergeants and privates, had that strong optimism, not based on any kind of reason; but gradually it died out, and in its place came the awful conviction which settled upon the hearts of the fighting-men, that this war would go on forever, that it was their doom always to live in ditches and dugouts, and that their only way of escape was by a “Blighty” wound or by death.

A chaplain I knew used to try to cheer up despondent boys by pretending to have special knowledge of inside politics.

“I have it on good authority,” he said, “that peace is near at hand. There have been negotiations in Paris﻿—”

Or:

“I don’t mind telling you lads that if you get through the next scrap you will have peace before you know where you are.”

They were not believing, now. He had played that game too often.

“Old stuff, padre!” they said.

That particular crowd did not get through the next scrap. But the padre’s authority was good. They had peace long before the armistice.

---

It was worst of all for boys of sensitive minds who were lucky enough to get a “cushie” wound, and so went on and on, or who were patched up again quickly after one, two, or three wounds, and came back again. It was a boy like that who revealed his bitterness to me one day as we stood together in the salient.

===Chinese===

起初，开战之初，我们的官兵相信它会速了。我们的第一支远征军开到法国时喊着快活的口号「用不了多久咱就回家！」——随后他们从蒙斯退到马恩河，退开德国人推进的潮水，像秋叶一样凋落了青春。随后去的新军男孩们发疯般想赶上「大冒险」，咒骂英国营地里训练之长。「等咱们出去就晚啦！」他们说。晚了，天哪！甚至等他们头一轮进过战壕、撞上德国人的实力之后，他们还一时抱一种古怪的信心：会有「什么事」发生，让和平像战争来时一样快地到来。和平永远走在前面三个月。将军和参谋军官，同军士和列兵一样，抱着那种不基于任何道理的强烈乐观；可它渐渐死掉了，取代它的是落到作战人心上那个可怕的定见：这场战争会永远打下去，住壕沟地洞是他们的命，逃出去的路只有一条——「回国伤」，或者死。

我认得的一位随军牧师惯于装作有内幕政治消息，好给丧气的男孩们打气。

「我有可靠的消息，」他说，「和平近在眼前。巴黎已经谈过——」

或者：

「不瞒你们说，小子们，只要你们熬过下一仗，回头还没弄清身在哪儿，和平就到了。」

如今他们不信了。这一手他玩得太多次。

「老掉牙了，神父！」他们说。

那一伙人没能熬过下一仗。可神父的消息不假。他们早在停战之前就得到和平了。

---

最苦的是那些心性敏感、侥幸得了「软伤」于是活下去的男孩，或一处两处三处伤后很快补好又回来的。就是这样一个男孩，一天同我一起站在突出部上，向我吐了他的苦水。

===Original===

“It’s the length of the war,” he said, “which does one down. At first it seemed like a big adventure, and the excitement of it, horrible though it was, kept one going. Even the first time I went over the top wasn’t so bad as I thought it would be. I was dazed and drunk with all sorts of emotions, including fear, that were worse before going over. I had what we call ‘the needle.’ They all have it. Afterward one didn’t know what one was doing﻿—even the killing part of the business﻿—until one reached the objective and lay down and had time to think and to count the dead about﻿ ﻿… Now the excitement has gone out of it, and the war looks as though it would go on forever. At first we all searched the papers for some hope that the end was near. We don’t do that now. We know that whenever the war ends, this year or next, this little crowd will be mostly wiped out. Bound to be. And why are we going to die? That’s what all of us want to know. What’s it all about? Oh yes, I know the usual answers: ‘In defense of liberty,’ ‘To save the Empire.’ But we’ve all lost our liberty. We’re slaves under shellfire. And as for the Empire﻿—I don’t give a curse for it. I’m thinking only of my little home at Streatham Hill. The horrible Hun? I’ve no quarrel with the poor blighters over there by Hooge. They are in the same bloody mess as we are. They hate it just as much. We’re all under a spell together, which some devils have put on us. I wonder if there’s a God anywhere.”

---

This sense of being under a black spell I found expressed by other men, and by German prisoners who used the same phrase. I remember one of them in the battles of the Somme, who said, in good English: “This war was not made in any sense by mankind. We are under a spell.” This belief was due, I think, to the impersonal character of modern warfare, in which gunfire is at so long a range that shellfire has the quality of natural and elemental powers of death﻿—like thunderbolts﻿—and men killed twenty miles behind the lines while walking over sunny fields or in busy villages had no thought of a human enemy desiring their individual death.

===Chinese===

「是战争的长，」他说，「把人拖垮。起初它像一场大冒险，那种兴奋——虽然可怕——撑着人。连我头一回越出壕顶，也不像想的那么坏。我被种种情绪——包括恐惧——震晕了、灌醉了，出击之前那才是最坏的。我犯了我们叫『打摆子』的毛病。人人都有。后来人不知道自己在干什么——连杀人的那一部分——直到冲上目标卧下来，才有工夫想，才有工夫数四周的死人……如今兴奋褪了，战争看着要永远打下去。起初我们都翻报纸找终点将至的希望。现在不翻了。我们知道，不管战争哪天结束，今年或明年，这一小伙人大半会被抹掉。注定如此。可我们凭什么去死？这是我们全都想知道的。这一切为了什么？哦，是，那些惯常的答案我都知道：『捍卫自由』，『拯救帝国』。可我们的自由早没了。我们是炮火下的奴隶。至于帝国——我他妈的一个子儿的在乎都不给它。我只想我斯特里特姆山的小家。可怕的德国佬？我同胡格那边那些可怜虫无冤无仇。他们同我们一样陷在这摊血污里。他们一样恨。我们全着了同一个咒，哪个魔鬼下的。我不知哪儿还有没有上帝。」

---

这种中了黑咒的感觉，我从别的人嘴里也听到过，德国俘虏用的是同一个词。我记得索姆河各役里的一个，用漂亮的英语说：「这场战争绝不是人类以任何方式造成的。我们着了咒。」我想，这信念源于现代战争的非人格性质：炮火射程那么远，炮击有了自然的、元素般的死亡之力——像霹雳——在战线后二十英里的人，走在阳光的田野上或忙碌的村子里被打死，绝不会想到有一个人的敌人存心要他个人的死。

===Original===

God and Christianity raised perplexities in the minds of simple lads desiring life and not death. They could not reconcile the Christian precepts of the chaplain with the bayoneting of Germans and the shambles of the battlefields. All this blood and mangled flesh in the fields of France and Flanders seemed to them﻿—to many of them, I know﻿—a certain proof that God did not exist, or if He did exist was not, as they were told, a God of Love, but a monster glad of the agonies of men. That at least was the thought expressed to me by some London lads who argued the matter with me one day, and that was the thought which our army chaplains had to meet from men who would not be put off by conventional words. It was not good enough to tell them that the Germans were guilty of all this crime and that unless the Germans were beaten the world would lose its liberty and life. “Yes, we know all that,” they said, “but why did God allow the Germans, or the statesmen who arranged the world by force, or the clergy who christened British warships? And how is it that both sides pray to the same God for victory? There must be something wrong somewhere.”

It was not often men talked like that, except to some chaplain who was a human, comradely soul, some Catholic “padre” who devoted himself fearlessly to their bodily and spiritual needs, risking his life with them, or to some Presbyterian minister who brought them hot cocoa under shellfire, with a cheery word or two, as I once heard, of “Keep your hearts up, my lads, and your heads down.”

---

Most of the men became fatalists, with odd superstitions in the place of faith. “It’s no good worrying,” they said.

“If your name is written on a German shell you can’t escape it, and if it isn’t written, nothing can touch you.”

Officers as well as men had this fatalistic belief and superstitions which amused them and helped them. “Have the Huns found you out yet?” I asked some gunner officers in a ruined farmhouse near Kemmel Hill. “Not yet,” said one of them, and then they all left the table at which we were at lunch and, making a rush for some oak beams, embraced them ardently. They were touching wood.

===Chinese===

上帝和基督教在渴望生不渴望死的单纯小伙子心里搅起了困惑。他们没法把随军牧师的基督教诫命同刺刀捅德国人、同战场的屠宰场调和起来。法兰西和佛兰德斯田野上这一切血和断肢残肉，在他们看来——我知道在许多人看来——是确凿的证据：上帝不存在；或者存在，也不像他们被告知的那样是爱的上帝，而是个以人的痛苦为乐的怪物。至少那是一天同一群伦敦小伙子辩论时他们对我说的，也是我们的随军牧师们必须面对的想法——面对这些不肯被套话打发的人。对他们说德国人负有这一切罪、德国人不被打败世界就失去自由和生命，是不够的。「是，这些我们都知道，」他们说，「可上帝为什么容许德国人？容许那些用武力安排世界的政客？容许那些给英国军舰行洗礼的教士？两边怎么能向同一个上帝祷告求胜？总有什么地方出了错。」

人不大这样说话，除非对某位通人性、够战友的牧师，某位无畏地献身于他们身体和灵魂需要、同他们一起冒险的天主教「神父」，或某位炮火下给他们送热可可的长老会牧师——带一两句快活话，像我听过的那句：「心放高些，小子们，头放低些。」

---

多数人成了宿命论者，用古怪的迷信顶替信仰。「担心没用，」他们说。

「你的名字要是写在一发德国炮弹上，躲不掉；要是没写，什么也碰不着你。」

军官同士兵一样有这种宿命信念和迷信，那逗乐他们，也帮助他们。「德国佬摸清你们了没？」在凯梅尔山附近一座破农舍里我问几个炮兵军官。「还没有，」其中一个说，随即他们全体离开了我们正吃午饭的桌子，冲向几根橡木梁，热烈地抱住它们。他们在摸木头。

===Original===

“Take this with you,” said an Irish officer on a night I went to Ypres. “It will help you as it has helped me. It’s my lucky charm.” He gave me a little bit of coal which he carried in his tunic, and he was so earnest about it that I took it without a smile and felt the safer for it.

Once in a while the men went home on seven days’ leave, or four, and then came back again, gloomily, with a curious kind of hatred of England because the people there seemed so callous to their suffering, so utterly without understanding, so “damned cheerful.” They hated the smiling women in the streets. They loathed the old men who said, “If I had six sons I would sacrifice them all in the Sacred Cause.” They desired that profiteers should die by poison-gas. They prayed God to get the Germans to send zeppelins to England﻿—to make the people know what war meant. Their leave had done them no good at all.

---

From a weekend at home I stood among a number of soldiers who were going back to the front, after one of those leaves. The boat warped away from the pier, the M.T.O. and a small group of officers, detectives, and Red Cross men disappeared behind an empty train, and the “revenants” on deck stared back at the cliffs of England across a widening strip of sea.

“Back to the bloody old trenches,” said a voice, and the words ended with a hard laugh. They were spoken by a young officer of the Guards, whom I had seen on the platform of Victoria saying goodbye to a pretty woman, who had put her hand on his shoulder for a moment, and said, “Do be careful, Desmond, for my sake!” Afterward he had sat in the corner of his carriage, staring with a fixed gaze at the rushing countryside, but seeing nothing of it, perhaps, as his thoughts traveled backward. (A few days later he was blown to bits by a bomb﻿—an accident of war.)

A little man on deck came up to me and said, in a melancholy way, “You know who I am, don’t you, sir?”

I hadn’t the least idea who he was﻿—this little ginger-haired soldier with a wizened and wistful face. But I saw that he wore the claret-colored ribbon of the V.C. on his khaki tunic. He gave me his name, and said the papers had “done him proud,” and that they had made a lot of him at home﻿—presentations, receptions, speeches, Lord Mayor’s addresses, cheering crowds, and all that. He was one of our Heroes, though one couldn’t tell it by the look of him.

===Chinese===

「把这个带上，」一个爱尔兰军官在我去伊普尔的那晚说。「它会帮你，像帮过我一样。是我的幸运符。」他给我一小块煤，装在他军衣里带的，说得那样恳切，我一丝笑也没带地收下了，还当真觉得安全了些。

偶尔，士兵们回家休七天假，或四天，然后再回来，阴沉沉地，怀着一种古怪的对英格兰的恨——因为那里的人对他们的苦难显得那么无动于衷，那么全然不解，那么「该死的兴高采烈」。他们恨街上微笑的女人。他们厌恶说「我有六个儿子就全献给神圣事业」的老头。他们盼发国难财的都中毒气死。他们求上帝叫德国人派齐柏林飞艇去英格兰——叫人民知道战争是什么。他们的假期对他们一点好处没有。

---

国内的一个周末之后，我夹在一群度完假回前线的士兵中间。船缆松开码头，运输军官和一小群军官、侦探、红十字会的人消失在一列空车后头，甲板上的「还魂人」回望英格兰的崖岸，中间隔着越拉越宽的一条海。

「回那血腥的老战壕去，」一个声音说，末了一声硬笑。说话的是近卫团的一个年轻军官，我曾在维多利亚站的月台上看见他同一个漂亮女人道别，她把一只手在他肩上放了一放，说：「千万小心，德斯蒙德，看在我的分上！」后来他缩在车厢一角，直瞪着飞掠的乡野，也许什么也没看见，思绪往回走。（几天之后他被一颗炸弹炸成碎块——战争的一桩意外。）

甲板上一个小个子朝我走来，忧郁地说：「您认得我，对吧，长官？」

我全然不知他是谁——这个姜黄头发、面容干瘦而怅惘的小个子士兵。可我看见他卡其军衣上系着维多利亚十字勋的紫红绶带。他报了名字，说报纸「捧够了他」，说家里把他大肆风光——授勋、酒会、演讲、市长致辞、欢呼的人群，全套。他是我们的英雄之一，虽然看长相瞧不出来。

===Original===

“Now I’m going back to the trenches,” he said, gloomily. “Same old business and one of the crowd again.” He was suffering from the reaction of popular idolatry. He felt hipped because no one made a fuss of him now or bothered about his claret-colored ribbon. The staff-officers, chaplains, brigade majors, regimental officers, and army nurses were more interested in an airship, a silver fish with shining gills and a humming song in its stomach.

France﻿ ﻿… and the beginning of what the little V.C. had called “the same old business.” There was the long fleet of motor-ambulances as a reminder of the ultimate business of all those young men in khaki whom I had seen drilling in the Embankment gardens and shouldering their way down the Strand.

Some stretchers were being carried to the lift which goes down to the deck of the hospital-ship, on which an officer was ticking off each wounded body after a glance at the label tied to the man’s tunic. Several young officers lay under the blankets on those stretchers and one of them caught my eye and smiled as I looked down upon him. The same old business and the same old pluck.

I motored down the long, straight roads of France eastward, toward that network of lines which are the end of all journeys after a few days’ leave, home and back again. The same old sights and sounds and smells which, as long as memory lasts, to men who had the luck to live through the war, will haunt them for the rest of life, and speak of Flanders.

The harvest was nearly gathered in, and where, a week or two before, there had been fields of high, bronzed corn there were now long stretches of stubbled ground waiting for the plow. The wheat-sheaves had been piled into stacks or, from many great fields, carted away to the red-roofed barns below the black old windmills whose sails were motionless because no breath of air stirred on this September afternoon. The smell of Flemish villages﻿—a mingled odor of sunbaked thatch and bakeries and manure heaps and cows and ancient vapors stored up through the centuries﻿—was overborne by a new and more pungent aroma which crept over the fields with the evening haze.

===Chinese===

「现在我回战壕去了，」他阴郁地说。「还是老一套，又做回人群中的一员。」他正犯民间偶像崇拜的反胃。因为眼下再没人围着他转、没人理会他的紫红绶带，他郁郁不乐。参谋军官们、牧师们、旅参谋长们、团军官们和军队护士们，更关心一艘飞艇——一条亮鳃闪银、肚子里嗡嗡唱歌的银鱼。

法兰西……小个子十字勋说的「老一套」开始了。长长的摩托救护车队在那里，提醒着我在河堤花园里操练、在河滨街上挤开人行的那些卡其青年的终极营生。

几副担架正抬向通往医院船甲板的升降机，船上一位军官看一眼系在伤员军衣上的标签，勾一个名字。担架的毯子下面躺着几个年轻军官，其中一个同我目光相遇，我俯视他时他朝我笑了笑。还是老一套，还是老一套的胆气。

我驱车沿法兰西笔直的长路向东，奔向那张线路的网——几天休假之后一切旅程的终点，回了家，再回来。还是老一套的景、声、味，只要记忆还在，对侥幸活过战争的人，它们将纠缠余生，说着佛兰德斯。

收获快完了，一两个星期前还是高大古铜的玉米田的地方，现在是一条条留茬的地，等着犁。麦捆垛成了垛，或从许多大田里运走，送进黑色老风车下面的红顶谷仓——风车的翼一动不动，因为这个九月的下午没有一丝风。佛兰德斯村庄的气味——晒热的茅草、面包房、粪堆、牛，和积攒了几世纪的古气，混成的一股——被一种新的、更冲的气味压过，它随傍晚的霾爬过田野。

===Original===

It was a sad, melancholy smell, telling of corruption and death. It was the first breath of autumn, and I shivered a little. Must there be another winter of war? The old misery of darkness and dampness was creeping up through the splendor of September sunshine.

Those soldiers did not seem to smell it, or, if their nostrils were keen, to mind its menace﻿—those soldiers who came marching down the road, with tanned faces. How fine they looked, and how hard, and how cheerful, with their lot! Speak to them separately and every man would “grouse” at the duration of the war and swear that he was “fed up” with it. Homesickness assailed them at times with a deadly nostalgia. The hammering of shellfire, which takes its daily toll, spoiled their temper and shook their nerves, as far as a British soldier had any nerves, which I used to sometimes doubt, until I saw again the shell-shock cases.

But again I heard their laughter and an old song whistled vilely out of tune, but cheerful to the tramp of their feet. They were going back to the trenches after a spell in a rest-camp, to the same old business of whizzbangs and pip-squeaks, and dugouts, and the smell of wet clay and chloride of lime, and the life of earthmen who once belonged to a civilization which had passed. And they went whistling on their way, because it was the very best thing to do.

One picked up the old landmarks again, and got back into the “feel” of the war zone. There were the five old windmills of Cassel that wave their arms up the hill road, and the estaminets by which one found one’s way down country lanes﻿—“The Veritable Cuckoo” and “The Lost Corner” and “The Flower of the Fields”﻿—and the first smashed roofs and broken barns which led to the area of constant shellfire. Ugh!

So it was still going on, this bloody murder! There were some more cottages down in the village, where we had tea a month before. And in the marketplace of a sleepy old town the windows were mostly broken and some shops had gone into dust and ashes. That was new since we last passed this way.

===Chinese===

那是一种悲哀的、忧伤的气味，诉着腐坏与死亡。那是秋天的第一口气，我微微一抖。难道还要再来一个战争之冬？黑暗与潮湿的旧苦难，正顺着九月阳光的壮丽往上爬。

那些士兵似乎闻不见它，或者鼻尖也闻得见、却不理会它的威胁——那些沿大路开下来的士兵，晒黑的脸。他们看着多好，多硬扎，对自己的命多快活！分开来同他们谈，个个都会为战争之久「发牢骚」，赌咒说自己「受够了」。乡愁时时以致命的怀乡病袭他们。炮火的锤打——每日抽它的份——搅了他们的脾气，震了他们的神经，就英国士兵还有神经而言——我从前常怀疑这一点，直到再看那些炮弹休克的病例。

可我又听见了他们的笑，一支老歌用口哨吹得极走调，却合着脚步、那么提气。他们休整营里过了一段，正回战壕去，回那嗖嗖弹和小尖叫、地洞、湿土和漂白粉气味的老一套，回那曾经属于一个逝去文明的穴居人的日子。他们一路吹着口哨走，因为那是再好不过的做法。

人又拾起老路标，找回战区的「感觉」。卡塞尔的五架老风车在坡道上挥着臂，乡下小路靠那些小酒馆辨认——「真布谷鸟」「迷角」「野花」——然后是头一批砸烂的屋顶和断仓，通向常炮火的地界。呃！
