加拿大骑步枪第一营的肖中校从坎伯兰地洞里收拢了八十人，战死了。德国人被顶了一阵，可他们把手榴弹扔进那方人阵，活下来的寥寥。只剩八个人还在战友的尸体间打的时候，帕尔默少校——他们中间最后的军官——下令这八个人撤退。

与此同时，支援的各营顶着同样狂怒的炮火守得牢牢的，德国步兵撞上来的正是加拿大人的这第二道线——撞碎了。

中路，德国人的矛头直指泽勒贝克湖。这里有些加拿大步枪兵作支援，步兵攻击一开始，他们奉命前出迎击敌人。指挥其中一个营的军官后来告诉我，他带人横穿野地去枫树丛，顶着的火力前所未见。因为前面的战友急需救援，伤员倒下无人顾得上管，其余的人只管能多快就多快地压上去。

到了枫树丛，人们停下，同已经守着这片六七英亩树林的另一个营一起等敌人。德国部队到时，也许以为遇不到大抵抗。他们遇上的是枯萎的火力，付出了血代价。加拿大人聚在各点，各点成了带机枪和炸弹库的坚强支撑，他们把火憋到敌人近前才放，在敌群中大开杀戒。可德国的炮不停，许多加拿大人倒下。加拿大议会议员贝克上校，胸口一块弹片，倒下了。

===Original===

Hour after hour our gunners fed their breeches and poured out shells. The edge of the salient was swept with fire, and, though the Canadian losses were frightful, the Germans suffered also, so that the battlefield was one great shambles. Our own wounded, who were brought back, owe their lives to the stretcher-bearers, who were supreme in devotion. They worked in and out across that shell-swept ground hour after hour through the day and night, rescuing many stricken men at a great cost in life to themselves. Out of one party of twenty only five remained alive. “No one can say,” said one of their officers, “that the Canadians do not know how to die.”

No one would deny that.

Out of three thousand men in the Canadian 8th Brigade their casualties were twenty-two hundred.

There were 151 survivors from the 1st Battalion Canadian Mounted Rifles, 130 from the 4th Battalion, 350 from the 5th, 520 from the 2nd. Those are the figures of massacre.

Eleven days later the Canadians took their revenge. Their own guns were but a small part of the huge orchestra of “heavies” and field batteries which played the devil’s tattoo upon the German positions in our old trenches. It was annihilating, and the German soldiers had to endure the same experience as their guns had given to Canadian troops on the same ground. Trenches already battered were smashed again. The earth, which was plowed with shells in their own attack, was flung up again by our shells. It was hell again for poor human wretches.

The Canadian troops charged at two o’clock in the morning. Their attack was directed to the part of the line from the southern end of Sanctuary Wood to Mount Gorst, about a mile, which included Armagh Wood, Observatory Hill, and Mount Gorst itself.

The attack went quickly and the men expected greater trouble. The enemy’s shellfire was heavy, but the Canadians got through under cover of their own guns, which had lengthened their fuses a little and continued an intense bombardment behind the enemy’s first line. The men advanced in open order and worked downward and southward into their old positions.

In one place of attack about forty Germans, who fought desperately, were killed almost to a man, just as Colonel Shaw had died on June 2nd with his party of eighty men who had rallied round him. It was one shambles for another, and the Germans were not less brave, it seems.

===Chinese===

一个钟头又一个钟头，我们的炮手喂着炮闩，倾泻炮弹。突出部的边被火扫着，虽然加拿大人损失骇人，德国人也同样遭殃，战场成了一片大屠宰场。我们被抬回来的伤员，命是担架兵给的，他们奉献到极致。他们日夜在那片弹扫的地上进进出出，一干多少个钟头，救下许多被击倒的人，自己付出重大的生命代价。一队二十人，活下来五个。「谁也不能说，」他们的一个军官说，「加拿大人不会死。」

没有人会否认。

加拿大第八旅三千人，伤亡两千二。

加拿大骑步枪第一营幸存 151 人，第四营 130 人，第五营 350 人，第二营 520。这些是屠杀的数字。

十一天后，加拿大人报了仇。他们自己的炮只是一小部分——庞大的重炮和野炮乐队在德军占据的我们的旧壅上敲着魔鬼的点子。那是歼灭性的，德国士兵不得不领受他们的炮在同一片地上给过加拿大部队的同样滋味。已经打烂的壅再被打烂。他们自己攻击时被炮弹犁过的土，又被我们的炮弹掀了一遍。可怜的人类生灵又是地狱。

加拿大部队凌晨两点冲锋。他们的攻击指向从圣所林南端到戈斯特山约一英里的一段线，含阿马林、天文台山和戈斯特山本身。

攻击进展快，士兵们原以为会更难。敌人的炮火重，可加拿大人靠自己炮群的掩护穿过去了——炮群稍稍延长了引信，在敌人一线背后继续猛轰。士兵以疏开队形推进，向下向南打回他们的旧阵地。

在一处攻击点，约四十个拼死抵抗的德国人几乎被打死殆尽，正像肖中校六月二日同他聚拢的八十人一起死那样。一场屠场换一场屠场，看来德国人也一样勇敢。

===Original===

One officer and one hundred and thirteen men surrendered. The officer was glad to escape from the death to which he had resigned himself when our bombardment began.

“I knew how it would be,” he said. “We had orders to take this ground, and took it; but we knew you would come back again. You had to do so. So here I am.”

Parts of the line were deserted, except by the dead. In one place the stores which had been buried by the Canadians before they left were still there, untouched by the enemy. Our bombardment had made it impossible for his troops to consolidate their position and to hold the line steady.

They had just taken cover in the old bits of trench, in shell-holes and craters, and behind scattered sandbags, and had been pounded there. The Canadians were back again.

===Chinese===

一名军官和一百一十三名士兵投降了。那军官庆幸逃出了他本来认定的死——我们的炮击一开始，他已把死认下了。

「我知道会这样，」他说。「我们奉命夺这块地，夺下了；可我们知道你们会打回来。你们必须打回来。所以我在这儿了。」

几段战线上空无一人，只有死人。有一处，加拿大人撤走前埋下的给养还原封在，敌人没动。我们的炮击使他们无法巩固阵地、稳住战线。

他们刚在旧壅的残段、弹坑和爆破坑里、零散的沙袋后躲定，就在那儿挨了锤。加拿大人回来了。

## Part / 部
===Original===

V

The Heart of a City

Amiens in Time of War

===Chinese===

V

一座城的心脏

战争时期的亚眠

### I / 一

### I /

### I /

### I / 
===Original===

During the battles of the Somme in 1916, and afterward in periods of progress and retreat over the abominable fields, the city of Amiens was the capital of the British army. When the battles began in July of that year it was only a short distance away from the fighting-lines; near enough to hear the incessant roar of gunfire on the French front and ours, and near enough to get, by motorcar or lorry, in less than thirty minutes, to places where men were being killed or maimed or blinded in the routine of the day’s work. One went out past Amiens station and across a little stone bridge which afterward, in the enemy’s advance of 1918, became the mark for German high velocities along the road to Querrieux, where Rawlinson had his headquarters of the Fourth Army in an old château with pleasant meadows round it and a stream meandering through fields of buttercups in summertime. Beyond the dusty village of Querrieux with its white cottages, from which the plaster fell off in blotches as the war went on, we went along the straight highroad to Albert, through the long and straggling village of Lahoussoye, where Scottish soldiers in reserve lounged about among frowsy peasant women and played solemn games with “the bairns”; and so, past camps and hutments on each side of the road, to the ugly redbrick town where the Golden Virgin hung head downward from the broken tower of the church with her Babe outstretched above the fields of death as though as a peace-offering to this world at war.

One could be killed any day in Albert. I saw men blown to bits there the day after the battles of the Somme began. It was in the road that turned to the right, past the square to go to Méaulte and on to Fricourt. There was a tide of gun transport swirling down the road, bringing up new ammunition for the guns that were firing without a pause over Fricourt and Mametz. The high scream of a shell came through a blue sky and ended on its downward note with a sharp crash. For a few minutes the transport column was held up while a mass of raw flesh which a second before had been two living men and their horses was cleared out of the way. Then the gun wagons went at a harder pace down the road, raising a cloud of white dust out of which I heard the curses of the drivers, swearing in a foul way to disguise their fear.

===Chinese===

一九一六年索姆河各战役期间，以及后来在那片可憎的原野上进退的时期，亚眠城是英国军队的都城。那年七月战役打响时，它离战线只有短短一段；近得听得见法军和我们前线不停歇的炮吼，近得坐汽车或卡车不到三十分钟就能到那些地方——人们正在那里按当天的例行工作被杀死、致残、打瞎。人出亚眠车站，过一座小石桥——后来一九一八年敌军推进时，那桥成了德国高速弹沿去克雷约的公路的标靶——罗林森的第四集团军司令部就设在克雷约一座老城堡里，四周宜人的草甸，夏天一条溪流蜿蜒穿过毛茛的田野。过了尘土的克雷约村——白村舍，随着战争拖长，墙皮一块块剥落——我们沿笔直的大路去阿尔贝，穿过拉乌索耶那个又长又散的村子，苏格兰预备兵在那里同邋遢的村妇闲逛，同「小娃儿」们玩郑重的游戏；就这样，过路两边的营地和棚屋，到那座丑陋的红砖城——金圣母头朝下悬在教堂断塔上，怀里的圣婴伸向死亡的田野，仿佛献给这个交战世界的一件和平祭。

在阿尔贝，人随便哪天都可能死。索姆河战役打响的第二天，我就在那里看见人被炸成碎块。就在右拐去梅奥尔特再去弗里库尔的那条路上。一股炮兵运输的潮水顺路卷过，给正对弗里库尔和马梅茨不停轰击的火炮送新弹药。一声炮弹的高啸穿过蓝天，落调一收，一声脆炸。运输队停了几分钟，把一团生肉清出道来——一秒钟前那还是两个活人和他们的马。随后炮车加紧赶路，卷起一团白尘，尘里我听见车夫们的咒骂，骂得脏，遮他们的怕。

===Original===

I went through Albert many scores of times to the battlefields beyond, and watched its process of disintegration through those years, until it was nothing but a wild scrap heap of red brick and twisted iron, and, in the last phase, even the Golden Virgin and her Babe, which had seemed to escape all shellfire by miraculous powers, lay buried beneath a mass of masonry. Beyond were the battlefields of the Somme where every yard of ground is part of the great graveyard of our youth.

===Chinese===

我几十次穿过阿尔贝去那边的战场，看着它那些年里的碎解过程，直到它只剩红砖和拧铁的野堆，最后阶段，连凭着神力似乎躲过了一切炮火的金圣母和她的圣婴，也埋进了一大堆砌体底下。再往前，就是索姆河的战场，那里每一码地都是我们青春那片大墓园的一部分。

===Original===

So Amiens, as I have said, was not far away from the red heart of war, and was clear enough to the lines to be crowded always with officers and men who came out between one battle and another, and by “lorry-jumping” could reach this city for a few hours of civilized life, according to their views of civilization. To these men﻿—boys, mostly﻿—who had been living in lousy ditches under hell fire, Amiens was Paradise, with little hells for those who liked them. There were hotels in which they could go get a bath, if they waited long enough or had the luck to be early on the list. There were streets of shops with plate-glass windows unbroken, shining, beautiful. There were well-dressed women walking about, with kind eyes, and children as dainty, some of them, as in High Street, Kensington, or Prince’s Street, Edinburgh. Young officers, who had plenty of money to spend﻿—because there was no chance of spending money between a row of blasted trees and a ditch in which bits of dead men were plastered into the parapet﻿—invaded the shops and bought fancy soaps, razors, hair-oil, stationery, pocketbooks, knives, flash-lamps, top-boots (at a fabulous price), khaki shirts and collars, gramophone records, and the latest set of Kirchner prints. It was the delight of spending, rather than the joy of possessing, which made them go from one shop to another in search of things they could carry back to the line﻿—that and the lure of girls behind the counters, laughing, bright-eyed girls who understood their execrable French, even English spoken with a Glasgow accent, and were pleased to flirt for five minutes with any group of young fighting-men﻿—who broke into roars of laughter at the gallantry of some Don Juan among them with the gift of audacity, and paid outrageous prices for the privilege of stammering out some foolish sentiment in broken French, blushing to the roots of their hair (though captains and heroes) at their own temerity with a girl who, in another five minutes, would play the same part in the same scene with a different group of boys.

===Chinese===

于是，如我说过，亚眠离战争的红色心脏不远，离战线又够空，总是挤满两仗之间出来的官兵，靠「跳卡车」几个钟头就摸到这座城，过一把文明生活——按他们对文明的理解。对这些人——多半是男孩——在地狱之火下的虱窝沟里住了好久的人来说，亚眠是天堂，还附带给喜欢者的几处小地狱。有旅馆，等得够久或运气好排在名单前头，就能洗上个澡。有整街的铺子，大玻璃橱窗不破，亮晶晶，美。有衣着一新的女人走来，眼睛和善，孩子精致，有的不输肯辛顿的高街或爱丁堡的王子街。年轻军官们钱多得花不完——因为在一排烧秃的树和一条把死人碎肉糊进胸墙的沟之间，没有花钱的机会——涌进了那些铺子，买香皂、剃刀、发油、文具、皮夹、小刀、手电、长筒靴（天价）、卡其衬衫和领子、唱片，还有最新一套基希纳版画。让他们挨店挨家跑的，是花的快乐，不是有的快乐——还有柜台后姑娘们的诱惑：爱笑、眼睛发亮，听得懂他们那糟透的法语，连格拉斯哥腔的英语也行，乐意同任何一小伙年轻作战人调情五分钟——小伙们为他们中间某个有胆量的唐璜的献殷情哄然大笑，为结巴着用破碎法语说傻话的特权付出离谱的价，脸红到发根（虽然身为上尉和英雄）——为自己的唐突害臊，而那姑娘五分钟后就将在同一幕戏里同另一伙男孩演同一个角色。

===Original===

I used to marvel at the patience of these girls. How bored they must have been with all this flirtation, which led to nothing except, perhaps, the purchase of a bit of soap at twice its proper price! They knew that these boys would leave to go back to the trenches in a few hours and that some of them would certainly be dead in a few days. There could be no romantic episode, save of a transient kind, between them and these good-looking lads in whose eyes there were desire and hunger, because to them the plainest girl was Womanhood, the sweet, gentle, and feminine side of life, as opposed to the cruelty, brutality, and ugliness of war and death. The shopgirls of Amiens had no illusions. They had lived too long in war not to know the realities. They knew the risks of transient love and they were not taking them﻿—unless conditions were very favorable. They attended strictly to business and hoped to make a lot of money in the shop, and were, I think, mostly good girls﻿—as virtuous as life in wartime may let girls be﻿—wise beyond their years, and with pity behind their laughter for these soldiers who tried to touch their hands over the counters, knowing that many of them were doomed to die for France and England. They had their own lovers﻿—boys in blue somewhere between Vaux-sur-Somme and Hartmanns-weilerkopf﻿—and apart from occasional intimacies with English officers quartered in Amiens for long spells, left the traffic of passion to other women who walked the streets.

===Chinese===

我常惊叹这些姑娘的耐心。这调情多叫她们腻啊——它通不到任何地方，顶多按双倍价卖出一块香皂！她们知道这些男孩几小时后就回战壕，其中一些人几天内必死。她们同这些漂亮小伙子之间不会有什么罗曼史，除了转瞬那一种，因为对他们，最平常的姑娘也是女人——生活里甜蜜、温柔、女性的一面，对着战争与死亡的残忍、粗暴和丑。亚眠的店娘们没有幻想。她们在战争里活得太久，懂现实。她们知道露水爱的风险，不冒——除非条件非常有利。她们严守生意，指望在店里挣一大笔；我想她们多半是好姑娘——战时的生活许可姑娘们怎么贞，她们就怎么贞——比她们的年纪懂事得多，笑声后面藏着可怜，可怜这些隔着柜台想碰她们手的士兵——知道他们中许多注定为法兰西和英格兰去死。她们有自己的爱人——蓝色军装的男孩，在索姆河畔沃和哈特曼斯韦勒峰之间的什么地方——除了同长驻亚眠的英国军官偶尔的亲近，把激情的买卖留给街上走的女人。

### II / 二

### II /

### II /

### II / 
===Original===

The Street of the Three Pebbles﻿—la rue des Trois Cailloux﻿—which goes up from the station through the heart of Amiens, was the crowded highway. Here were the best shops﻿—the hairdresser, at the left-hand side, where all day long officers down from the line came in to have elaborate luxury in the way of close crops with *friction d’eau de quinine*, shampooing, singeing, oiling, not because of vanity, but because of the joyous sense of cleanliness and perfume after the filth and stench of life in the desolate fields; then the booksellers’ (Madame Carpentier *et fille*) on the right-hand side, which was not only the rendezvous of the miscellaneous crowd buying stationery and *La Vie Parisienne*, but of the intellectuals who spoke good French and bought good books and liked ten minutes’ chat with the mother and daughter. (Madame was an Alsatian lady with vivid memories of 1870, when, as a child, she had first learned to hate Germans.) She hated them now with a fresh, vital hatred, and would have seen her own son dead a hundred times﻿—he was a soldier in Saloniki﻿—rather than that France should make a compromise peace with the enemy. She had been in Amiens, as I was, on a dreadful night of August of 1914, when the French army passed through in retreat from Bapaume, and she and the people of her city knew for the first time that the Germans were close upon them. She stood in the crowd as I did﻿—in the darkness, watching that French column pass with their transport, and their wounded lying on the baggage wagons, men of many regiments mixed up, the light of the street lamps shining on the casques of cuirassiers with their long horsehair tails, leading their stumbling horses, and foot soldiers, hunched under their packs, marching silently with dragging steps. Once in a while one of the soldiers left the ranks and came on to the sidewalk, whispering to a group of dark shadows. The crowds watched silently, in a curious, dreadful silence, as though stunned. A woman near me spoke in a low voice, and said, “*Nous sommes perdus!*” Those were the only words I heard or remembered.

===Chinese===

三石街——从车站上去、穿过亚眠心脏的那条——是拥挤的大道。这里有好铺子——左边理发店，从线上下来的军官全天拥进去，享受精致奢侈的贴头皮剪，加奎宁水摩擦、香洗、火燎、上油——不为虚荣，为的是荒凉田野生活的污秽恶臭之后，那种干净和香气的快活感；右边书铺（卡庞捷太太和女儿），它不但是买文具和《巴黎生活》的杂色人群的会合点，也是说法语的好、买好书的知识分子的——他们喜欢同母女俩聊十分钟。（太太是位阿尔萨斯淑女，对一八七〇年记忆鲜明，那时她还是孩子，头一回学会恨德国人。）如今她恨他们，恨得新鲜而有生气，宁愿自己的儿子死一百回——他在萨洛尼卡当兵——也不愿法兰西同敌人妥协媾和。一九一四年八月那个可怕的夜晚，她同我一样在亚眠，法军从巴波姆溃退经过，她和她城里的人头一回知道德国人近在身后。她同我一样站在人群里——黑暗中，看那支法国纵队带着辎重过，伤者躺在行李车上，许多团的人混着，街灯的光照在胸甲骑兵的盔上，马鬃垂着，牵着踉跄的马，步兵背着包弓着身，拖着步子默默行军。时不时有个士兵出列，走上人行道，对一群黑影低语。人群静静看着，一种古怪而可怕的静，像被打懵了。我身旁一个女人低声说：「Nous sommes perdus（我们完了）！」那是我听见或记得的唯一的话。

===Original===

That night in the station of Amiens the boys of a new class were being hurried away in truck trains, and while their army was in retreat sang “La Marseillaise,” as though victory were in their hearts. Next day the German army under von Kluck entered Amiens, and ten days afterward passed through it on the way to Paris. Madame Carpentier told me of the first terror of the people when the field-gray men came down the Street of the Three Pebbles and entered their shops. A boy selling oranges fainted when a German stretched out his hand to buy some. Women hid behind their counters when German boots stamped into their shops. But Madame Carpentier was not afraid. She knew the Germans and their language. She spoke frank words to German officers, who saluted her respectfully enough. “You will never get to Paris﻿ ﻿… France and England will be too strong for you﻿ ﻿… Germany will be destroyed before this war ends.” They laughed at her and said: “We shall be in Paris in a week from now. Have you a little diary, Madame?” Madame Carpentier was haughty with them. Some women of Amiens﻿—poor drabs﻿—did not show any haughtiness, nor any pride, with the enemy who crowded into the city on their way toward Paris. A girl told me that she was looking through the window of a house that faced the Place de la Gare, and saw a number of German soldiers dancing round a piano-organ which was playing to them. They were dancing with women of the town, who were laughing and screeching in the embrace of big, blond Germans. The girl who was watching was only a schoolgirl then. She knew very little of the evil of life, but enough to know that there was something in this scene degrading to womanhood and to France. She turned from the window and flung herself on her bed and wept bitterly﻿ ﻿…

===Chinese===

那天夜里，亚眠车站上，新一届的男孩们正被塞进敞车急急运走，他们的军队在溃退中，他们唱着《马赛曲》，仿佛胜利在胸。第二天，冯·克卢克麾下的德军进了亚眠，十天后取道它去巴黎。卡庞捷太太对我讲过灰野战服的人顺着三石街下来、走进铺子时，人们最初的恐怖。一个卖橙子的男孩，一个德国人伸手要买时，晕倒了。德国靴子踏进铺子时，女人们躲到柜台后。可卡庞捷太太不怕。她认得德国人，会他们的话。她对德国军官说直话，军官们对她倒相当恭敬。「你们到不了巴黎……法兰西和英格兰对你们太强了……这场战争结束前德国就会被毁掉。」他们笑她，说：「一周后我们就在巴黎了。您有小日历册么，太太？」卡庞捷太太对他们高傲。亚眠有些女人——可怜的邋遢货——对涌进城、取道去巴黎的敌人，没有显出高傲，也没有显出自尊。一个姑娘告诉我，她从面朝车站广场的一扇窗里望出去，看见一群德国兵围着一架替他们演奏的手摇风琴跳舞。同他们跳的是城里的野鸡，在大个子金发德国人的怀抱里笑着尖叫。看的那个姑娘当时只是个女学生。人生的恶她懂得很少，可已够她知道这一幕里有辱没女人、辱没法兰西的东西。她从窗前转过身，扑在床上，痛苦地哭了……

===Original===

I used to call in at the bookshop for a chat now and then with Madame and Mademoiselle Carpentier, while a crowd of officers came in and out. Madame was always merry and bright in spite of her denunciations of the “*Sale Boches﻿—les brigands, les bandits!*” and Mademoiselle put my knowledge of French to a severe but pleasant test. She spoke with alarming rapidity, her words tumbling over one another in a cascade of volubility delightful to hear but difficult to follow. She had a strong mind﻿—masterly in her methods of business﻿—so that she could serve six customers at once and make each one think that her attention was entirely devoted to his needs﻿—and a very shrewd and critical idea of military strategy and organization. She had but a poor opinion of British generals and generalship, although a wholehearted admiration for the gallantry of British officers and men; and she had an intimate knowledge of our preparations, plans, failures, and losses. French liaison-officers confided to her the secrets of the British army; and English officers trusted her with many revelations of things “in the wind.” But Mademoiselle Carpentier had discretion and loyalty and did not repeat these things to people who had no right to know. She would have been far more efficient as a staff officer than many of the young gentlemen with red tabs on their tunics who came into the shop, flipping beautiful top-boots with riding-crops, sitting on the counter, and turning over the pages of *La Vie* for the latest convention in ladies’ legs.

Mademoiselle was a serious musician, so her mother told me, but her musical studies were seriously interrupted by business and air raids, which one day ceased in Amiens altogether after a night of horror, when hundreds of houses were smashed to dust and many people killed, and the Germans brought their guns close to the city﻿—close enough to scatter high velocities about its streets﻿—and the population came up out of their cellars, shaken by the terror of the night, and fled. I passed the bookshop where Mademoiselle was locking up the door of this house which had escaped by greater luck than its neighbors. She turned as I passed and raised her hand with a grave gesture of resignation and courage. “*Ils ne passeront pas!*” she said. It was the spirit of the courage of French womanhood which spoke in those words.

===Chinese===

我常去书铺，同卡庞捷太太和小姐聊一阵，军官们进进出出。太太永远轻快乐观，尽管骂着「Sale Boches（脏波希）——强盗！土匪！」，小姐则把我的法语架在严厉而愉快的火上烤。她说得吓人地快，词一个绊一个，滔滔的瀑布，好听，难追。她头脑强干——生意手法大师级——能同时招呼六个客人，让每个都觉得她的注意力全归他——对军事战略和组织又有一套精明挑剔的见解。她对英国将军和将道评价不高，虽然对英国官兵的英勇全心钦佩；对我们的准备、计划、失败和损失，她了如指掌。法国联络军官向她吐英军的秘密；英国军官们把许多「风闻」托付给她。可卡庞捷小姐有分寸有忠心，不把这些讲给无权知道的人。她当参谋军官，比许多进店来的、军衣上缀红领章、拿马鞭抽着漂亮长筒靴、坐上柜台、翻《巴黎生活》看女士大腿最新款式的年轻绅士强得多。

小姐是位严肃的音乐家——她母亲告诉我——可她的音乐学业被生意和空袭严重打断；有一天空袭在亚眠彻底停了，在恐怖的一夜之后——几百座房屋砸成灰，许多人死，德国人把炮拖到城边——近得高速弹撒进街道——人们从地窖里上来，被夜的恐怖震着，逃了。我经过书铺，小姐正锁门——这座宅子比邻居们运气好，逃过了。我经过时她转过身，抬起手，一个庄重的听任与勇气的手势。「Ils ne passeront pas（他们过不去）！」她说。那是法兰西女性勇气的精神，借着那几个字说话。

### III / 三

### III /

### III /

### III / 
===Original===

That was in the last phase of the war, but the Street of the Three Pebbles had been tramped up and down for two years before then by the British armies on the Somme, with the French on their right. I was never tired of watching those crowds and getting into the midst of them, and studying their types. All the types of young English manhood came down this street, and some of their faces showed the strain and agony of war, especially toward the end of the Somme battles, after four months or more of slaughter. I saw boys with a kind of hunted look in their eyes; and Death was the hunter. They stared into the shop windows in a dazed way, or strode along with packs on their backs, looking neither to the right nor to the left, and white, haggard faces, as expressionless as masks. Tomorrow or the next day, perhaps, the Hunter would track them down. Other English officers showed no sign at all of apprehension or lack of nerve-control, although the psychologist would have detected disorder of soul in the rather deliberate note of hilarity with which they greeted their friends, in gusts of laughter, for no apparent cause, at “Charlie’s bar,” where they would drink three cocktails apiece on an empty stomach, and in their tendency to tell tales of horror as things that were very funny. They dined and wined in Amiens at the “Rhin,” the “Godebert,” or the “Cathédrale,” with a kind of spiritual exaltation in good food and drink, as though subconsciously they believed that this might be their last dinner in life, with good pals about them. They wanted to make the best of it﻿—and damn the price. In that spirit many of them went after other pleasures﻿—down the byways of the city, and damned the price again, which was a hellish one. Who blames them? It was war that was to blame, and those who made war possible.

Down the rue des Trois Cailloux, up and down, up and down, went English, and Scottish, and Irish, and Welsh, and Canadian, and Australian, and New Zealand fighting-men. In the winter they wore their trench-coats all splashed and caked up to the shoulders with the white, chalky mud of the Somme battlefields, and their top-boots and puttees were plastered with this mud, and their faces were smeared with it after a lorry drive or a tramp down from the line. The rain beat with a metallic tattoo on their steel hats. Their packs were all sodden.

===Chinese===

那是战争的末段，可在那之前两年，三石街已被索姆河的英国各军、连同右翼的法国人，上上下下踏了个遍。我看不厌那些人群，爱钻进他们中间，研究他们的类型。年轻的英格兰男性，一切类型都下到这条街上来，有些脸带着战争的紧绷和苦痛，尤其在索姆河各役近尾声时，四个多月屠杀之后。我见过眼里带着一种被追猎神色的男孩；死亡是那猎手。他们发懵地瞪着橱窗，或背着包大步走，左右不看，脸白而憔悴，面具似的没有表情。明天或后天，猎手也许就追到他们。另一些英国军官，全无 apprehension 或失禁的迹象，虽然心理学家会从那相当刻意的高兴调子里——问候朋友时那种、无缘无故一阵阵的笑、在「查利酒吧」空着肚子一人三杯鸡尾酒、把恐怖的事当大笑话讲的倾向里——查出灵魂的乱。他们在亚眠的「莱茵」「戈德贝」或「大教堂」吃喝，带着一种精神的昂扬就着好饭好酒，仿佛潜意识里相信这可能是此生最后一顿晚餐，身边围着好伙伴。他们要尽兴——价钱见鬼去。带着这股精神，他们中许多人去寻别的乐——下到城的小巷深处，再把价钱咒一遍——那是地狱般的价。谁怪他们？该怪的是战争，和那些使战争成为可能的人。

三石街上，上上下下，上上下下，走着英格兰、苏格兰、爱尔兰、威尔士、加拿大、澳大利亚、新西兰的作战人。冬天他们穿着战壕大衣，齐肩溅满结着索姆河战场白垩泥的泥壳，长筒靴和绑腿糊满这种泥，坐卡车或从线上走下来后，脸上也抹着它。雨点在钢盔上敲出金属的点子。他们的背包全湿透了。

===Original===

French poilus, detrained at Amiens station for a night on their way to some other part of the front, jostled among British soldiers, and their packs were a wonder to see. They were like traveling tinkers, with pots and pans and boots slung about their faded blue coats, and packs bulging with all the primitive needs of life in the desert of the battlefields beyond civilization. They were unshaven, and wore their steel casques low over their foreheads, without gaiety, without the means of buying a little false hilarity, but grim and sullen-looking and resentful of English soldiers walking or talking with French cocottes.

===Chinese===

法国大兵们在亚眠站下车，去前线别处途中过一夜，在英国兵中间挤来挤去，他们的背包看得人啧啧称奇。他们像走方的补锅匠，褪色的蓝军衣四周吊着锅、盆和靴子，背包鼓着文明之外的战场荒漠里一切原始的必需。他们没刮脸，钢盔低压着前额，没有快活，没有买一点虚假兴奋的钱，阴沉乖戾，见了同法国粉头并肩走或说话的英国兵就来气。

### IV / 四

### IV /

### IV /

### IV / 
===Original===

I saw a scene with a French poilu one day in the Street of the Three Pebbles, during those battles of the Somme, when the French troops were fighting on our right from Maricourt southward toward Roye. It was like a scene from *Gaspard*. The poilu was a middle-aged man, and very drunk on some foul spirit which he had bought in a low café down by the river. In the High Street he was noisy, and cursed God for having allowed the war to happen, and the French government for having sentenced him and all poor *sacré poilus* to rot to death in the trenches, away from their wives and children, without a thought for them; and nothing but treachery in Paris:

“*Nous sommes trahis!*” said the man, raising his arms. “For the hundredth time France is betrayed.”

A crowd gathered round him, listening to his drunken denunciations. No one laughed. They stared at him with a kind of pitying wonderment. An *agent de police* pushed his way between the people and caught hold of the soldier by the wrist and tried to drag him away. The crowd murmured a protest, and then suddenly the poilu, finding himself in the hands of the police, on this one day out of the trenches﻿—after five months﻿—flung himself on the pavement in a passion of tears and supplication.

“*Je suis père de famille!﻿ ﻿… Je suis un soldat de France!﻿ ﻿… Dans les tranchées pour cinq mois!﻿ ﻿… Qu’est-ce que mes camarades vont dire, ’cré nom de Dieu? et mon capitaine? C’est emmordant après toute ma service comme brave soldat. Mais, quoi donc, mon vieux!*”

“*Viens donc, saligaud*,” growled the *agent de police*.

The crowd was against the policeman. Their murmurs rose to violent protest on behalf of the poilu.

“*C’est un héros, tout de même. Cinq mois dans les tranchées! C’est affreux! Mais oui, il est soûl, mais pour-quoi pas! Après cinq mois sur le front qu’est-ce que cela signifie? Ça n’a aucune importance!*”

A dandy French officer of Chasseurs Alpins stepped into the center of the scene and tapped the policeman on the shoulder.

“Leave him alone. Don’t you see he is a soldier? Sacred name of God, don’t you know that a man like this has helped to save France, while you pigs stand at street corners watching petticoats?”

He stooped to the fallen man and helped him to stand straight.

“Be off with you, *mon brave*, or there will be trouble for you.”

He beckoned to two of his own Chasseurs and said:

===Chinese===

索姆河各役期间，法国部队在我们右翼从马丽库尔往南朝鲁瓦打的时候，一天我在三石街看见一个法国大兵的一幕，像《加斯帕》里的一幕。那大兵是个中年人，灌了河下一家低级咖啡馆的什么劣酒，醉得很。在大街上他闹起来，咒上帝不该放战争发生，咒法国政府判他、判所有可怜的大兵们在战壕里烂死，离开老婆孩子，没人管他们的死活；巴黎除了背叛没有别的：

「Nous sommes trahis（我们被出卖了）！」那人举起胳膊说。「法兰西第一百次被出卖。」

人群围拢来，听他的醉骂。没人笑。他们带着一种怜悯的惊奇瞪他。一个警察挤进人堆，抓住士兵的手腕，想拖他走。人群咕哝着抗议，那大兵忽然发觉自己落进警察手里——五个月后出壕的这一天——扑倒在人行道上，泪水与哀告齐发。

「Je suis père de famille（我是一家之父）！……Je suis un soldat de France（我是法兰西的士兵）！……Dans les tranchées pour cinq mois（壕沟里蹲了五个月）！……我的战友们会怎么说，他妈的？还有我的上尉？当了这么多年好兵，落这么个下场。可是，怎么着呢，老伙计！」

「走，臭流氓，」警察低吼。

人群向着大兵，反对警察。咕哝升成了替大兵的激烈抗议。

「他到底是英雄。壕沟里五个月！惨极了！是，他醉了，可凭什么不醉！前线五个月之后，这算个什么事？一点也不要紧！」

一位花花公子式的阿尔卑斯猎兵军官踏进场景中央，拍拍警察的肩。

「放开他。没看见他是士兵么？神圣的名号，你不知道这样的人帮着救了法兰西，你们这些猪却站在街角看裙子？」

他俯身扶起跌倒的人，帮他站直。

「去吧，好汉，不然你要吃麻烦。」

他朝自己两个猎兵招招手，说：

===Original===

“Look after that poor comrade yonder. He is *un peu étoilé*.”

The crowd applauded. Their sympathy was all for the drunken soldier of France.

===Chinese===

「照看那边那位可怜的战友。他有点儿上头了。」

人群鼓掌。他们的同情全在法兰西的醉兵那边。

### V / 五

### V /

### V /

### V / 
===Original===

Into a small estaminet at the end of the rue des Trois Cailloux, beyond the Hôtel de Ville, came one day during the battles of the Somme two poilus, grizzled, heavy men, deeply bronzed, with white dust in their wrinkles, and the earth of the battlefields ingrained in the skin of their big, coarse hands. They ordered two “little glasses” and drank them at one gulp. Then two more.

“See what I have got, my little cabbage,” said one of them, stooping to the heavy pack which he had shifted from his shoulders to the other seat beside him. “It is something to make you laugh.”

“And what is that, my old one?” said a woman sitting on the other side of the marble-topped table, with another woman of her own class, from the market nearby.

The man did not answer the question, but fumbled into his pack, laughing a little in a self-satisfied way.

“I killed a German to get it,” he said. “He was a pig of an officer, a dirty Boche. Very chic, too, and young like a schoolboy.”

One of the women patted him on the shoulder. Her eyes glistened.

“Did you slit his throat, the dirty dog? Eh, I’d like to get my fingers round the neck of a dirty Boche!”

“I finished him with a grenade,” said the poilu. “It was good enough. It knocked a hole in him as large as a cemetery. See then, my cabbage. It will make you smile. It is a funny kind of mascot, eh?”

He put on the table a small leather pouch stained with a blotch of reddish brown. His big, clumsy fingers could hardly undo the little clasp.

“He wore this next his heart,” said the man. “Perhaps he thought it would bring him luck. But I killed him all the same! *’Cré nom de Dieu!*”

He undid the clasp, and his big fingers poked inside the flap of the pouch.

“It was from his woman, his German grue. Perhaps even now she doesn’t know he’s dead. She thinks of him wearing this next to his heart. *’Cré nom de Dieu!* It was I that killed him a week ago!”

He held up something in his hand, and the light through the estaminet window gleamed on it. It was a woman’s lock of hair, like finespun gold.

===Chinese===

索姆河各役期间的一天，两个大兵走进三石街尽头、市政厅过去一点的一家小酒馆：灰白头发的壮汉，晒得深褐，皱纹里嵌着白尘，粗大手掌的皮肤里长进去了战场的土。他们要了两小杯，一口干了。又来两杯。

「瞧我拿到了什么，我的小卷心菜，」其中一个说着，弯腰去够他从肩上卸到旁边座位上的重背包。「有个东西保你笑。」

「是什么呀，我的老头儿？」大理石桌对面一个女人说，同她一起的还有同类的另一个，都是近旁市场来的。

那人不答，往背包里掏，自得地笑着。

「我杀了个德国佬才弄到的，」他说。「是个军官猪，脏波希。还挺俊，像个学童。」

一个女人拍拍他的肩。她的眼放光。

「你割了他喉咙了，脏狗？呃，我也想拿手指掐住一个脏波希的脖子！」

「我一颗手榴弹送了他，」大兵说。「够本了。在他身上开了一个坟地大的窟窿。看哪，我的卷心菜。保管你笑。这是一种好笑的吉祥物，嗯？」

他把一只小皮袋放上桌，一块红褐的渍斑染着它。粗大的手指笨拙地解那小小的搭扣。

「他把它贴心口戴着，」那人说。「大概指望它给他好运。可我还是杀了他！他妈的！」

他解开搭扣，粗手指伸进袋盖里掏。

「是他女人给的，他的德国婆娘。说不定这会儿她还不知道他死了。她还想着他把它贴心口戴着呢。他妈的！一星期前杀他的，是我！」

他手里举起一样东西，酒馆窗透进的光在它上面闪。是一绺女人的头发，细纺的金。

===Original===

The two women gave a shrill cry of surprise, and then screamed with laughter. One of them tried to grab the hair, but the poilu held it high, beyond her reach, with a gruff command of, “Hands off!” Other soldiers and women in the estaminet gathered round staring at the yellow tress, laughing, making ribald conjectures as to the character of the woman from whose head it had come. They agreed that she was fat and ugly, like all German women, and a foul slut.

“She’ll never kiss *that* fellow again,” said one man. “Our old one has cut the throat of that pig of a Boche!”

“I’d like to cut off all her hair and tear the clothes off her back,” said one of the women. “The dirty drab with yellow hair! They ought to be killed, every one of them, so that the human race should be rid of them!”

“Her lover is a bit of clay, anyhow,” said the other woman. “A bit of dirt, as our poilus will do for all of them.”

The soldier with the woman’s hair in his hand stroked it across his forefinger.

“All the same it is pretty. Like gold, eh? I think of the woman, sometimes. With blue eyes, like a German girl I kissed in Paris﻿—a dancing-girl!”

There was a howl of laughter from the two women.

“The old one is drunk. He is amorous with the German cow!”

“I will keep it as a mascot,” said the poilu, scrunching it up and thrusting it into his pouch. “It’ll keep me in mind of that *saligaud* of a German officer I killed. He was a chic fellow, *tout de même*. A boy.”

===Chinese===

两个女人发出一声尖利的惊叫，随后笑得尖叫。其中一个想抢那绺头发，大兵把它高高举起，够不着，粗声下令：「手拿开！」酒馆里别的士兵和女人围拢来，瞪着那绺金发，笑着，对它主人的品性作下流的猜想。他们一致断定她又肥又丑，同所有德国女人一样，是个脏货。

「她再也亲不上那家伙了，」一个男人说。「咱老头子把那头波希猪的喉咙割了！」

「我真想剃光她的头发，撕掉她身上的衣裳，」一个女人说。「黄毛的脏货！她们全该杀，一个不留，叫人类除掉这一族！」

「她的情人反正是块泥了，」另一个女人说。「一块烂泥，咱的大兵们会把他们全都办成那样。」

手里攊着女人头发的士兵把它在食指上抹了一下。

「可它到底好看。像金子，嗯？我有时想那女人。蓝眼睛，像我在巴黎亲过的一个德国姑娘——跳舞的！」

两个女人一阵大笑。

「老头子醉了。他对那头德国母牛动情啦！」

「我留着它当吉祥物，」大兵说着，把它团起来塞进皮袋。「好叫我想起我杀掉的那个流氓德国军官。他到底是个俊家伙。一个孩子。」

### VI / 六

### VI /

### VI / 
===Original===

Australians slouched up the Street of the Three Pebbles with a grim look under their wide-brimmed hats, having come down from Pozières, where it was always hell in the days of the Somme fighting. I liked the look of them, dusty up to the eyes in summer, muddy up to their eyes in winter﻿—these gipsy fellows, scornful of discipline for discipline’s sake, but desperate fighters, as simple as children in their ways of thought and speech (except for frightful oaths), and looking at life, this life of war and this life in Amiens, with frank, curious eyes, and a kind of humorous contempt for death, and disease, and English Tommies, and French girls, and “the whole damned show,” as they called it. They were lawless except for the laws to which their souls gave allegiance. They behaved as the equals of all men, giving no respect to generals or staff-officers or the devils of hell. There was a primitive spirit of manhood in them, and they took what they wanted, and were ready to pay for it in coin or in disease or in wounds. They had no conceit of themselves in a little, vain way, but they reckoned themselves the only fighting-men, simply, and without boasting. They were hard as steel, and finely tempered. Some of them were ruffians, but most of them were, I imagine, like those English yeomen who came into France with the Black Prince, men who lived “rough,” close to nature, of sturdy independence, good-humored, though fierce in a fight, and ruthless. That is how they seemed to me, in a general way, though among them were boys of a more delicate fiber, and sensitive, if one might judge by their clear-cut features and wistful eyes. They had money to spend beyond the dreams of our poor Tommy. Six shillings and sixpence a day and remittances from home. So they pushed open the doors of any restaurant in Amiens and sat down to table next to English officers, not abashed, and ordered anything that pleased their taste, and wine in plenty.

===Chinese===

澳大利亚人压着宽檐帽沿下一张冷峻的脸，三石街上晃着上来——他们从波济耶尔下来，索姆河打仗的那些日子，那里永远是地狱。我喜欢他们的模样，夏天灰到眼，冬天泥到眼——这些吉卜赛家伙，蔑视为纪律而纪律的纪律，却是拼死的战士，思想和说话的方式（可怕的粗口除外）简单得像孩子，用坦白、好奇的眼睛看生活——这战争的生活和这亚眠的生活——带着一种对死亡、疾病、英国汤米、法国姑娘、以及「整个该死的大戏」——他们这么叫——的幽默的蔑视。他们无法无天，除了他们灵魂效忠的法。他们行事同人人平等，对将军、参谋军官、乃至地狱的魔鬼一概不给尊敬。他们身上有一种原始的男子汉精神，想要什么就拿什么，准备用钱、病或伤偿付。他们没有小里小气的虚荣自恋，只把自己径直算作唯一的作战人，不带吹嘘。他们硬如钢，淬得好。有些是无赖，可我想大多数像当年随黑太子进法兰西的那些英格兰自耕农——活得「粗」，贴着自然，独立倔强，和气，打起来凶，狠。大体上他们给我的是这个印象，虽然他们中间也有纤维更细、更敏感的男孩——从清秀的轮廓和怅惆的眼睛判断。他们的钱多到我们可怜的汤米做梦想不到。一天六先令六便士，外加家里汇款。于是他们推开亚眠随便哪家馆子的门，在英国军官邻座坐下，毫不激然，点一切合口味的菜，酒管够。

===Original===

In that High Street of Amiens one day I saw a crowd gathered round an Australian, so tall that he towered over all other heads. It was at the corner of the rue de Corps Nu sans Teste, the Street of the Naked Body without a Head, and I suspected trouble. As I pressed on the edge of the crowd I heard the Australian ask, in a loud, slow drawl, whether there was any officer about who could speak French. He asked the question gravely, but without anxiety. I pushed through the crowd and said:

“I speak French. What’s the trouble?”

I saw then that, like the French poilu I have described, this tall Australian was in the grasp of a French *agent de police*, a small man of whom he took no more notice than if a fly had settled on his wrist. The Australian was not drunk. I could see that he had just drunk enough to make his brain very clear and solemn. He explained the matter deliberately, with a slow choice of words, as though giving evidence of high matters before a court. It appeared that he had gone into the estaminet opposite with four friends. They had ordered five glasses of *porto*, for which they had paid twenty centimes each, and drank them. They then ordered five more glasses of *porto* and paid the same price, and drank them. After this they took a stroll up and down the street, and were bored, and went into the estaminet again, and ordered five more glasses of *porto*. It was then the trouble began. But it was not the Australian who began it. It was the woman behind the bar. She served five glasses more of *porto* and asked for thirty centimes each.

“Twenty centimes,” said the Australian. “*Vingt, Madame.*”

“*Mais non! Trente centimes, chaque verre!* Thirty, my old one. *Six sous, comprenez?*”

“No comprennye,” said the Australian. “*Vingt* centimes, or go to hell.”

The woman demanded the thirty centimes; kept on demanding with a voice more shrill.

“It was her voice that vexed me,” said the Australian. “That and the bloody injustice.”

The five Australians drank the five glasses of *porto*, and the tall Australian paid the thirty centimes each without further argument. Life is too short for argument. Then, without words, he took each of the five glasses, broke it at the stem, and dropped it over the counter.

“You will see, sir,” he said, gravely, “the justice of the matter on my side.”

===Chinese===

有一天在亚眠那条大街上，我看见一群人围着一个澳大利亚人，他高得越过所有别的头。就在「无头裸体街」的街角，我疑心出事了。挤到人群边上，我听见那澳大利亚人用又响又慢的拖腔问，附近有没有会讲法语的军官。他问得郑重，不焦急。我拨开人群说：

「我讲法语。什么事？」

于是我看见，同我描写过的那个法国大兵一样，这高个澳大利亚人被一个法国警察抓着——小个子，他对他的注意不超过落在腕上的一只苍蝇。澳大利亚人没醉。我看得出来他喝得刚好够脑子又清又庄重。他不慌不忙地解释事情，选词选得慢，像在法庭上就重大事项作证。事情是：他同四个朋友进了对面那家酒馆。他们要了五杯波尔图，一杯付了二十生丁，喝了。又要了五杯波尔图，同价，付了，喝了。随后他们上街溜达了一趟，无聊，又回进酒馆，再要五杯波尔图。麻烦就在这时开始。可先动手的不是澳大利亚人，是柜台后的女人。她又上了五杯波尔图，一杯要三十生丁。

「二十生丁，」澳大利亚人说。「Vingt（二十），Madame（太太）。」

「Mais non（不）！Trente centimes, chaque verre（三十生丁，一杯）！三十，我的老头儿。Six sous（六个苏），comprenez（懂么）？」

「不懂，」澳大利亚人说。「Vingt 生丁，不然见鬼去。」

女人非要三十不可，嗓门一声比一声尖。

「是她的嗓门惹了我，」澳大利亚人说。「还有那 bloody 的不公。」

五个澳大利亚人喝掉了那五杯波尔图，高个澳大利亚人不再争，一杯三十生丁照付。人生太短，不够吵架。随后，一言不发，他把五只杯子一只只齐颈折断，隔柜台丢了过去。

「您看得出来，长官，」他庄重地说，「道理在我这边。」

===Original===

But when they left the estaminet the woman came shrieking into the street after them. Hence the *agent de police* and the grasp on the Australian’s wrist.

“I should be glad if you would explain the case to this little Frenchman,” said the soldier. “If he does not take his hand off my wrist I shall have to kill him.”

“Perhaps a little explanation might serve,” I said.

I spoke to the *agent de police* at some length, describing the incident in the café. I took the view that the lady was wrong in increasing the price so rapidly. The *agent* agreed gravely. I then pointed out that the Australian was a very large-sized man, and that in spite of his quietude he was a man in the habit of killing Germans. He also had a curious dislike of policemen.

“It appears to me,” I said, politely, “that for the sake of your health the other end of the street is better than this.”

The *agent de police* released his grip from the Australian’s wrist and saluted me.

“*Vous avez raison, monsieur. Je vous remercie. Ces Australiens sont vraiment formidables, n’est-ce pas?*”

He disappeared through the crowd, who were smiling with a keen sense of understanding. Only the lady of the estaminet was unappeased.

“They are bandits, these Australians!” she said to the world about her.

The tall Australian shook hands with me in a comradely way.

“Thanks for your trouble,” he said. “It was the injustice I couldn’t stick. I always pay the right price. I come from Australia.”

I watched him go slouching down the rue des Trois Cailloux, head above all the passersby. He would be at Pozières again next day.
